papers.core_contribution: Identifies a trade-off between improving truthfulness and maintaining safety in LLMs, and proposes a method using sparse autoencoders to disentangle refusal and hallucination features, preserving the refusal subspace during fine-tuning to mitigate the trade-off.
papers.conclusion: There is a trade-off between truthfulness and refusal alignment in LLMs, and the proposed method using sparse autoencoders to disentangle features and preserve the refusal subspace during fine-tuning can maintain safety while preventing hallucinations from increasing.
papers.key_findings:
Truthfulness-enhancing edits (e.g., ITI, TruthX) increase jailbreak susceptibility, revealing a trade-off between factuality and safety.
Hallucination and refusal behaviors share overlapping internal representations in specific attention heads.
Fine-tuning on benign datasets can degrade safety alignment due to shared representational space between refusal and hallucination features.
The proposed SAE-guided fine-tuning method preserves refusal behavior while improving task utility, mitigating the trade-off.
papers.limitation:
Further investigation is needed to interpret how different alignment methods affect knowledge suppression and whether their impact varies across model architectures.
The analysis primarily examined specific components; a more comprehensive study of additional layers and mechanisms may yield deeper insights.
The proposed solution relies on a trained SAE, which may limit its practicality for fine-tuning at scale.
papers.abstract: Hallucination in large language models (LLMs) has been widely studied in recent years, with progress in both detection and mitigation aimed at improving truthfulness. Yet, a critical side effect remains largely overlooked: enhancing truthfulness can negatively impact safety alignment. In this paper, we investigate this trade-off and show that increasing factual accuracy often comes at the cost of weakened refusal behavior. Our analysis reveals that this arises from overlapping components in the model that simultaneously encode hallucination and refusal information, leading alignment methods to suppress factual knowledge unintentionally. We further examine how fine-tuning on benign datasets, even when curated for safety, can degrade alignment for the same reason. To address this, we propose a method that disentangles refusal-related features from hallucination features using sparse autoencoders, and preserves refusal behavior during fine-tuning through subspace orthogonalization. This approach prevents hallucinations from increasing while maintaining safety alignment.We evaluate our method on commonsense reasoning tasks and harmful benchmarks (AdvBench and StrongReject). Results demonstrate that our approach preserves refusal behavior and task utility, mitigating the trade-off between truthfulness and safety.

papers.title: Dynamic Attention-Guided Context Decoding for Mitigating Context Faithfulness Hallucinations in Large Language Models
papers.research_question: Why do large language models fail to faithfully utilize retrieved context (context faithfulness hallucinations), and how can token-level uncertainty and attention mechanisms be leveraged to mitigate this issue?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes Dynamic Attention-Guided Context Decoding (DAGCD), a lightweight decoding framework that leverages attention distributions and token-level uncertainty signals in a single pass to improve context faithfulness in LLM generation.
papers.conclusion: DAGCD effectively mitigates context faithfulness hallucinations by integrating attention-based context utilization signals and entropy-guided uncertainty adjustments during generation, providing a lightweight and efficient solution for context-sensitive tasks.
papers.key_findings:
A strong correlation exists between higher token-level uncertainty (entropy) and context faithfulness hallucinations.
Attention distributions inherently encode robust signals for context utilization, as validated by a probing classifier achieving high AUC.
DAGCD consistently improves faithfulness metrics (EM, F1) across multiple open-book QA datasets and model families without additional training.
The method is data-efficient, requiring only 100 training samples for the detector, and maintains performance across different prompt templates.
DAGCD operates in a single decoding pass, offering computational efficiency over multi-pass correction methods.
papers.limitation:
Performance may degrade with extremely long contexts, complex dialogues, or noisy/adversarial inputs due to reliance on the attention-ratio classifier.
The scaling factor α requires empirical calibration for different models, as the relationship between entropy and uncertainty is not quantitatively fixed.
Evaluation primarily focused on QA tasks; generalization to other tasks like summarization or dialogue requires further validation.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) often exhibit Context Faithfulness Hallucinations, where outputs deviate from retrieved information due to incomplete context integration. Our analysis reveals a strong correlation between token-level uncertainty and hallucinations. We hypothesize that attention mechanisms inherently encode context utilization signals, supported by probing analysis. Based on these insights, we propose Dynamic Attention-Guided Context Decoding (DAGCD), a lightweight framework that leverages attention distributions and uncertainty signals in a single-pass decoding. Experiments on open-book QA datasets demonstrate DAGCD's effectiveness, yielding significant improvements in faithfulness and robustness while preserving computational efficiency.

papers.title: HIME: Mitigating Object Hallucinations in LVLMs via Hallucination Insensitivity Model Editing
papers.research_question: How much intervention is necessary at each layer to suppress hallucinations while preserving pre-trained knowledge in Large Vision-Language Models?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces HIME, a training-free, layer-adaptive weight editing method that uses the Hallucination Insensitivity Score to selectively suppress hallucination subspaces in LVLMs, reducing hallucinations without additional overhead.
papers.conclusion: HIME effectively mitigates object hallucination in LVLMs via layer-adaptive weight editing guided by the Hallucination Insensitivity Score, achieving consistent hallucination reduction across benchmarks without introducing additional parameters, inference-time latency, or computational overhead.
papers.key_findings:
HIME reduces object hallucinations by an average of 61.8% across open-ended generation benchmarks.
Layer-wise analysis reveals non-uniform susceptibility to hallucination across decoder layers in LVLMs.
HIME outperforms prior decoding- and editing-based approaches on CHAIR, MME, and GPT-4V-aided evaluation.
HIME preserves or improves model utility (e.g., BLEU and MME perception scores) while mitigating hallucinations.
The Hallucination Insensitivity Score (HIS) effectively quantifies layer-wise hallucination sensitivity and guides targeted intervention.
papers.abstract: Large Vision-Language Models (LVLMs) have demonstrated impressive multimodal understanding capabilities, yet they remain prone to object hallucination, where models describe non-existent objects or attribute incorrect factual information, raising serious concerns for reliable real-world deployment. While fine-tuning is a commonly adopted mitigation strategy, its high computational cost and practical difficulty motivate the need for training-free alternatives, among which model editing has recently emerged as a promising direction. However, indiscriminate editing risks disrupting the rich implicit knowledge encoded in pre-trained LVLMs, leading to a fundamental question: how much intervention is necessary at each layer to suppress hallucinations while preserving pre-trained knowledge? To address this question, we present a systematic analysis of LVLM decoders built on three widely used large language model backbones-Qwen, LLaMA, and Vicuna-revealing clear layer-wise differences in susceptibility to object hallucination. Building on these insights, we introduce the Hallucination Insensitivity Score (HIS), a principled metric that quantifies each layer's sensitivity to hallucination and provides guidance for targeted intervention. Leveraging HIS, we propose Hallucination Insensitivity Model Editing (HIME), a simple yet effective layer-adaptive weight editing approach that selectively modifies latent features to suppress hallucinations while preserving pre-trained knowledge. Extensive experiments demonstrate that HIME reduces hallucinations by an average of 61.8% across open-ended generation benchmarks, including CHAIR, MME, and GPT-4V-aided evaluation, without introducing additional parameters, inference-time latency, or computational overhead.

papers.title: HIDE and Seek: Detecting Hallucinations in Language Models via Decoupled Representations
papers.research_question: Can we leverage the internal representations of LMs to detect hallucinations effectively and efficiently in a single-pass, training-free setting?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes HIDE, a single-pass, training-free method for hallucination detection that quantifies the statistical decoupling between an LM's internal representations of input and output sequences using an adapted Hilbert-Schmidt Independence Criterion (HSIC).
papers.conclusion: Measuring internal representational dependence is a promising direction for developing efficient and reliable hallucination detection systems, aiding in building more trustworthy LMs.
papers.key_findings:
HIDE outperforms other single-pass detection methods, achieving an average relative improvement of ~29% in AUC-ROC.
HIDE is competitive with multi-pass state-of-the-art methods, achieving an average relative improvement of ~3% in AUC-ROC while reducing computation time by ~51%.
HIDE's performance is robust across different transformer layers and kernel choices.
HIDE effectively detects both faithfulness and factuality hallucinations across diverse QA datasets and model scales.
The method requires only a single generation pass, making it efficient for real-time deployment.
papers.limitation: HIDE may struggle when input and output are lexically similar but semantically different, or when the model generates multiple correct answers, reducing the discriminative power of the dependence measure.
future_direction: Extending HIDE to multimodal settings.
Improving token selection strategies for more robust representation extraction.
Exploring the integration of HIDE with other detection paradigms for enhanced performance.
papers.abstract: Contemporary Language Models (LMs), while impressively fluent, often generate content that is factually incorrect or unfaithful to the input context - a critical issue commonly referred to as 'hallucination'. This tendency of LMs to generate hallucinated content undermines their reliability, especially because these fabrications are often highly convincing and therefore difficult to detect. While several existing methods attempt to detect hallucinations, most rely on analyzing multiple generations per input, leading to increased computational cost and latency. To address this, we propose a single-pass, training-free approach for effective Hallucination detectIon via Decoupled rEpresentations (HIDE). Our approach leverages the hypothesis that hallucinations result from a statistical decoupling between an LM's internal representations of input context and its generated output. We quantify this decoupling using the Hilbert-Schmidt Independence Criterion (HSIC) applied to hidden-state representations extracted while generating the output sequence. We conduct extensive experiments on four diverse question answering datasets, evaluating both faithfulness and factuality hallucinations across six open-source LMs of varying scales and properties. Our results demonstrate that HIDE outperforms other single-pass methods in almost all settings, achieving an average relative improvement of ~29% in AUC-ROC over the best-performing single-pass strategy across various models and datasets. Additionally, HIDE shows competitive and often superior performance with multi-pass state-of-the-art methods, obtaining an average relative improvement of ~3% in AUC-ROC while consuming ~51% less computation time. Our findings highlight the effectiveness of exploiting internal representation decoupling in LMs for efficient and practical hallucination detection.

papers.title: Seeing Clearly by Layer Two: Enhancing Attention Heads to Alleviate Hallucination in LVLMs
papers.research_question: How does the pattern of attention sinks in image tokens relate to hallucinations in multimodal large language models (MLLMs), and can enhancing attention heads in shallow layers alleviate hallucinations?
papers.core_contribution: This paper introduces Enhancing Attention Heads (EAH), a training-free, plug-and-play method that reduces hallucinations in multimodal large language models by identifying and broadcasting the attention map of the head with the densest vision sink in shallow layers.
papers.conclusion: EAH is an effective, training-free, and plug-and-play method for alleviating hallucinations in MLLMs by enhancing attention heads in shallow layers, as validated by extensive benchmark tests and generalization experiments.
papers.key_findings:
Hallucinations in MLLMs are linked to sparse attention sinks in image tokens; denser vision sinks in shallow layers correlate with fewer hallucinations.
The proposed EAH method, which broadcasts the attention map of the head with the densest vision sink to other heads in shallow layers, effectively reduces hallucinations across multiple models and benchmarks.
EAH improves performance on general vision-language tasks without additional computation, demonstrating its plug-and-play convenience and generalization ability.
The method also shows consistent gains in large language models (LLMs) on tasks like GSM8K and TruthfulQA, indicating broader applicability.
Ablation studies confirm that the optimal intervention occurs at layer 2 with a specific threshold, and broadcasting to all heads in the layer yields the best results.
papers.limitation: EAH exhibits about a 4 percentage point lower recall compared to other methods at the same average output length.
future_direction: Improved alignment of projectors and advanced training methods, such as reinforcement learning from human feedback (RLHF), are needed for more fundamental resolution of hallucination issues.
papers.abstract: The hallucination problem in multimodal large language models (MLLMs) remains a common issue. Although image tokens occupy a majority of the input sequence of MLLMs, there is limited research to explore the relationship between image tokens and hallucinations. In this paper, we analyze the distribution of attention scores for image tokens across each layer and head of the model, revealing an intriguing and common phenomenon: most hallucinations are closely linked to the pattern of attention sinks in the self-attention matrix of image tokens, where shallow layers exhibit dense attention sinks and deeper layers show sparse attention sinks. We further analyze the attention heads of different layers and find that heads with high-density attention sink in the image part play a positive role in alleviating hallucinations. In this paper, we propose a training-free method named \textcolor{red}{\textbf{E}}nhancing \textcolor{red}{\textbf{A}}ttention \textcolor{red}{\textbf{H}}eads (EAH), an approach designed to enhance the convergence of image tokens attention sinks in the shallow layers. EAH identifies the attention head that shows the vision sink in a shallow layer and extracts its attention matrix. This attention map is then broadcast to other heads in the layer, thereby strengthening the layer to pay more attention to the image itself. With extensive experiments, EAH shows significant hallucination-mitigating performance on different MLLMs and metrics, proving its effectiveness and generality.

papers.title: Stochastic Chameleons: Irrelevant Context Hallucinations Reveal Class-Based (Mis)Generalization in LLMs
papers.research_question: What is the nature of errors in large language models when they are given irrelevant context, and do these errors exhibit regularities?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that LLMs exhibit class-based (mis)generalization when integrating irrelevant context, and mechanistic analysis reveals that this arises from hierarchical class representations and competing circuits in the model's internal computations.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that LLMs are 'stochastic chameleons' that generalize by leveraging class structures and adapting to context, but in unreliable ways.
papers.key_findings:
Irrelevant context causes systematic changes in model predictions (answer change rate ~38-48%).
A majority (70%) of these changes align with class-based generalization.
Logit attribution shows hierarchical class-to-instance predictions.
Activation patching reveals competing circuits for context and query features.
Attention knockout can flip predictions, confirming the competition.
papers.limitation:
Experiments are conducted in a controlled setting, which may not fully reflect naturally occurring text.
The study is limited to English-language datasets.
Only models of certain sizes (7–8B, 12B, 70B) are evaluated.
Mechanistic interpretability focuses on layer-wise analysis, leaving attention head analysis for future work.
The study does not develop mitigation methods for contextual hallucinations.
future_direction: Designing setups that disentangle memorization and generalization in naturally occurring text.
Extending the analysis to smaller models and non-English datasets.
Conducting attention head analysis and developing mitigation methods informed by the findings.
papers.abstract: The widespread success of large language models (LLMs) on NLP benchmarks has been accompanied by concerns that LLMs function primarily as stochastic parrots that reproduce texts similar to what they saw during pre-training, often erroneously. But what is the nature of their errors, and do these errors exhibit any regularities? In this work, we examine irrelevant context hallucinations, in which models integrate misleading contextual cues into their predictions. Through behavioral analysis, we show that these errors result from a structured yet flawed mechanism that we term class-based (mis)generalization, in which models combine abstract class cues with features extracted from the query or context to derive answers. Furthermore, mechanistic interpretability experiments on Llama-3, Mistral, and Pythia across 39 factual recall relation types reveal that this behavior is reflected in the model's internal computations: (i) abstract class representations are constructed in lower layers before being refined into specific answers in higher layers, (ii) feature selection is governed by two competing circuits -- one prioritizing direct query-based reasoning, the other incorporating contextual cues -- whose relative influences determine the final output. Our findings provide a more nuanced perspective on the stochastic parrot argument: through form-based training, LLMs can exhibit generalization leveraging abstractions, albeit in unreliable ways based on contextual cues -- what we term stochastic chameleons.

papers.title: LANCET: Neural Intervention via Structural Entropy for Mitigating Faithfulness Hallucinations in LLMs
papers.research_question: How to mitigate faithfulness hallucinations in LLMs through precise neural intervention without harming general reasoning abilities?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes Lancet, a topological intervention framework that uses structural entropy to surgically block hallucination propagation pathways in LLMs, effectively mitigating faithfulness hallucinations without sacrificing factuality.
papers.conclusion: Lancet provides a topological approach to neural intervention that effectively mitigates faithfulness hallucinations by modeling them as infectious flows, achieving state-of-the-art performance while preserving model capabilities.
papers.key_findings:
Lancet significantly improves both faithfulness and factuality scores compared to state-of-the-art methods like TruthX and ITI.
The framework successfully isolates hallucination propagation pathways using structural entropy, minimizing collateral damage to general reasoning.
Ablation studies confirm that Hallucination Difference Ratio (HDR) and Structural Entropy (SE) are critical components for effective intervention.
Parameter sensitivity analysis reveals an optimal selection ratio and spatial decay factor for balancing intervention strength and model preservation.
Lancet generalizes well across different models like LLaMA2-7B-Chat and DeepSeek-llm-7B.
papers.limitation: Reliance on paired data and graph partitioning overhead presents scalability challenges
future_direction: Unsupervised instigator detection
Lightweight approximations to streamline the process
papers.abstract: Large Language Models have revolutionized information processing, yet their reliability is severely compromised by faithfulness hallucinations. While current approaches attempt to mitigate this issue through node-level adjustments or coarse suppression, they often overlook the distributed nature of neural information, leading to imprecise interventions. Recognizing that hallucinations propagate through specific forward transmission pathways like an infection, we aim to surgically block this flow using precise structural analysis. To leverage this, we propose Lancet, a novel framework that achieves precise neural intervention by leveraging structural entropy and hallucination difference ratios. Lancet first locates hallucination-prone neurons via gradient-driven contrastive analysis, then maps their propagation pathways by minimizing structural entropy, and finally implements a hierarchical intervention strategy that preserves general model capabilities. Comprehensive evaluations across hallucination benchmark datasets demonstrate that Lancet significantly outperforms state-of-the-art methods, validating the effectiveness of our surgical approach to neural intervention.

papers.title: On Early Detection of Hallucinations in Factual Question Answering
papers.research_question: Whether model artifacts (like token attributions, softmax probabilities, attention scores, and activations) can provide signals for detecting hallucinations in factual question answering.
papers.core_contribution: Model artifacts (softmax probabilities, attention scores, activations, and token attributions) can be used to detect hallucinations in factual question answering, and hallucinations can be detected even before they occur (at the first generation token).
papers.conclusion: Attaching classifiers based on model artifacts can flag potentially incorrect information before it reaches end-users, providing an effective method for hallucination detection.
papers.key_findings:
The distributions of model artifacts (softmax probabilities, attention scores, activations, token attributions) differ between hallucinated and non-hallucinated generations.
Classifiers using these artifacts can achieve up to 0.80 AUROC in detecting hallucinations.
Hallucinations can be detected at the first generation token, i.e., before the model generates the full answer.
Self-attention scores and fully-connected activations provide the best performance (more than 0.70 AUROC for most model-dataset pairs).
Integrated Gradients attributions perform poorly, often close to random.
papers.limitation:
The method cannot be used with blackbox models that do not reveal internals.
Only considered factual hallucinations and a simple setup with single facts.
Did not experiment with more elaborate retrieval settings, instruction tuned models, etc.
future_direction: Extending the method to other forms of hallucinations.
Extending to multiple hallucinations in a single generation.
Experimenting with more elaborate retrieval settings, instruction tuned models, in-context examples, wider range of datasets and model types.
papers.abstract: While large language models (LLMs) have taken great strides towards helping humans with a plethora of tasks, hallucinations remain a major impediment towards gaining user trust. The fluency and coherence of model generations even when hallucinating makes detection a difficult task. In this work, we explore if the artifacts associated with the model generations can provide hints that the generation will contain hallucinations. Specifically, we probe LLMs at 1) the inputs via Integrated Gradients based token attribution, 2) the outputs via the Softmax probabilities, and 3) the internal state via self-attention and fully-connected layer activations for signs of hallucinations on open-ended question answering tasks. Our results show that the distributions of these artifacts tend to differ between hallucinated and non-hallucinated generations. Building on this insight, we train binary classifiers that use these artifacts as input features to classify model generations into hallucinations and non-hallucinations. These hallucination classifiers achieve up to $0.80$ AUROC. We also show that tokens preceding a hallucination can already predict the subsequent hallucination even before it occurs.

papers.title: InterpDetect: Interpretable Signals for Detecting Hallucinations in Retrieval-Augmented Generation
papers.research_question: Can interpretable mechanistic signals (External Context Score and Parametric Knowledge Score) be used to build efficient and generalizable hallucination detectors for Retrieval-Augmented Generation systems?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces a method for detecting hallucinations in RAG by using interpretable mechanistic signals (External Context Score and Parametric Knowledge Score) derived from model internals, which are shown to be effective and generalizable across models.
papers.conclusion: Mechanistic signals provide efficient, generalizable predictors for hallucination detection in RAG systems, enabling low-cost evaluation of large-scale models.
papers.key_findings:
Hallucinations in RAG arise when later-layer FFN modules disproportionately inject parametric knowledge into the residual stream while attention underweights retrieved content.
External Context Score (ECS) and Parametric Knowledge Score (PKS) are effective features for training classifiers to detect hallucinated spans in RAG outputs.
Classifiers trained on mechanistic signals extracted from a small model (Qwen3-0.6b) can generalize to detect hallucinations in responses from larger, production-level models (GPT-4.1-mini).
The proposed method achieves competitive performance with commercial detection systems while being more computationally efficient.
The model exhibits higher recall than precision, which is argued to be desirable for downstream verification tasks.
papers.limitation:
Computing ECS and PKS across all layers and heads is computationally intensive, especially during the projection from hidden states to the vocabulary distribution.
The overall detection performance remains below that of large-scale models.
The proxy-based evaluation framework is insufficient for real-time response intervention, which would require access to and manipulation of layer-level activations.
future_direction: Identify the layers most critical for efficient hallucination detection to reduce computation.
Expand the feature set to include uncertainty-based measures and representation-level features to improve detection accuracy.
Apply mechanistic signals for response intervention to produce more reliable and truthful outputs.
papers.abstract: Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) integrates external knowledge to mitigate hallucinations, yet models often generate outputs inconsistent with retrieved content. Accurate hallucination detection requires disentangling the contributions of external context and parametric knowledge, which prior methods typically conflate. We investigate the mechanisms underlying RAG hallucinations and find they arise when later-layer FFN modules disproportionately inject parametric knowledge into the residual stream. To address this, we explore a mechanistic detection approach based on external context scores and parametric knowledge scores. Using Qwen3-0.6b, we compute these scores across layers and attention heads and train regression-based classifiers to predict hallucinations. Our method is evaluated against state-of-the-art LLMs (GPT-5, GPT-4.1) and detection baselines (RAGAS, TruLens, RefChecker). Furthermore, classifiers trained on Qwen3-0.6b signals generalize to GPT-4.1-mini responses, demonstrating the potential of proxy-model evaluation. Our results highlight mechanistic signals as efficient, generalizable predictors for hallucination detection in RAG systems.

papers.title: HARP: Hallucination Detection via Reasoning Subspace Projection
papers.research_question: Can the hidden state space of LLMs be decomposed into semantic and reasoning subspaces, and can projecting onto the reasoning subspace improve hallucination detection?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes HARP, a hallucination detection method that projects hidden states onto a reasoning subspace derived via SVD on the unembedding layer, achieving state-of-the-art performance.
papers.conclusion: HARP is an effective and robust method for hallucination detection by leveraging reasoning subspace projection, demonstrating superior accuracy and generalization.
papers.key_findings:
The hidden state space of LLMs can be decomposed into a direct sum of a semantic subspace and a reasoning subspace.
The Unembedding layer can disentangle these subspaces, and SVD on its parameters yields basis vectors for each.
Projecting hidden states onto the reasoning subspace reduces feature dimension to ~5% of the original, filtering noise and improving robustness.
HARP outperforms existing hallucination detection methods across multiple datasets and models.
A reasoning subspace dimension of about 5% of the hidden state dimension yields optimal detection performance.
future_direction: Hallucination mitigation by modifying reasoning subspace components.
papers.abstract: Hallucinations in Large Language Models (LLMs) pose a major barrier to their reliable use in critical decision-making. Although existing hallucination detection methods have improved accuracy, they still struggle with disentangling semantic and reasoning information and maintaining robustness. To address these challenges, we propose HARP (Hallucination detection via reasoning subspace projection), a novel hallucination detection framework. HARP establishes that the hidden state space of LLMs can be decomposed into a direct sum of a semantic subspace and a reasoning subspace, where the former encodes linguistic expression and the latter captures internal reasoning processes. Moreover, we demonstrate that the Unembedding layer can disentangle these subspaces, and by applying Singular Value Decomposition (SVD) to its parameters, the basis vectors spanning the semantic and reasoning subspaces are obtained. Finally, HARP projects hidden states onto the basis vectors of the reasoning subspace, and the resulting projections are then used as input features for hallucination detection in LLMs. By using these projections, HARP reduces the dimension of the feature to approximately 5% of the original, filters out most noise, and achieves enhanced robustness. Experiments across multiple datasets show that HARP achieves state-of-the-art hallucination detection performance; in particular, it achieves an AUROC of 92.8% on TriviaQA, outperforming the previous best method by 7.5%.

papers.title: Exposing Hallucinations To Suppress Them: VLMs Representation Editing With Generative Anchors
papers.research_question: Can we design a training-free, self-supervised method to mitigate hallucinations in multimodal large language models without sacrificing informativeness?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes a training-free, self-supervised method for hallucination mitigation in MLLMs by using dual visual anchors (original image and a reconstructed image from a text-to-image model) to edit decoder hidden states, pulling representations toward faithful semantics and pushing them away from hallucination directions.
papers.conclusion: The proposed training-free, self-supervised method effectively mitigates hallucinations in MLLMs without sacrificing informativeness, shows strong generalization across architectures, and serves as a practical plug-and-play module for building more faithful and reliable models.
papers.key_findings:
The method significantly reduces hallucinations at object, attribute, and relation levels while largely preserving recall and caption richness.
It demonstrates strong cross-architecture generalization across different MLLM models (e.g., LLaVA, Cambrian, InstructBLIP).
When applied to hallucination-free captions, the method introduces almost no side effects, showing robustness and plug-and-play applicability.
The dual-supervision editing mechanism (positive anchor from original image, negative anchor from reconstructed image) achieves an effective trade-off between faithfulness and informativeness.
The hallucination amplification mechanism using a text-to-image model effectively exposes implicit hallucinations, making them detectable for correction.
papers.limitation:
The method relies on the fidelity of the text-to-image (T2I) model, which may introduce noise, especially for fine-grained attributes like color.
There is an inherent trade-off between hallucination mitigation and preserving informativeness/recall.
Layer selection for latent editing is fixed (e.g., third layer) and not adaptive to input characteristics.
future_direction: Explore adaptive strategies for layer selection based on input characteristics or model states.
Integrate stronger generative backbones or develop selective filtering strategies to reduce noise from imperfect T2I reconstructions.
Investigate more principled ways to balance the trade-off, such as adaptive weighting schemes or context-aware editing strategies.
papers.abstract: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) have achieved remarkable success across diverse vision-language tasks, yet they remain highly susceptible to hallucinations, producing content that is fluent but inconsistent with visual evidence. Such hallucinations, spanning objects, attributes, and relations, persist even in larger models, while existing mitigation approaches often require additional finetuning, handcrafted priors, or trade-offs that compromise informativeness and scalability. To address this limitation, we propose a training-free, self-supervised method for hallucination mitigation. Our approach introduces a novel hallucination amplification mechanism: a caption is projected into the visual space via a text-to-image model to reveal implicit hallucination signals, serving as a negative anchor, while the original image provides a positive anchor. Leveraging these dual anchors, we edit decoder hidden states by pulling representations toward faithful semantics and pushing them away from hallucination directions. This correction requires no human priors or additional training costs, ensuring both effectiveness and efficiency. Extensive experiments across multiple benchmarks show that our method significantly reduces hallucinations at the object, attribute, and relation levels while largely preserving recall and caption richness, e.g., achieving a hallucination reduction by over 5% using LLaVA-v1.5-7B on CHAIR. Furthermore, results on diverse architectures, including LLaVA-NEXT-7B, Cambrian-8B, and InstructBLIP-7B, validate strong cross-architecture generalization. More importantly, when applied to hallucination-free captions, our method introduces almost no side effects, underscoring its robustness and practical plug-and-play applicability. The implementation will be publicly available.

papers.title: Can LLMs Lie? Investigation beyond Hallucination
papers.research_question: This paper investigates whether LLMs can intentionally lie (as opposed to unintentionally hallucinate), and how to understand and control lying behavior using mechanistic interpretability.
papers.core_contribution: The paper uncovers the neural mechanisms of lying in LLMs using mechanistic interpretability, and introduces steering vectors to control lying behavior, showing a trade-off between honesty and task performance.
papers.conclusion: The paper demonstrates that lying in LLMs can be understood and controlled via mechanistic interpretability, and highlights the trade-offs between honesty and task success in real-world scenarios.
papers.key_findings:
Lying ability in LLMs improves with model size and reasoning capabilities.
LLMs use dummy tokens as a computational scratchpad for lying, with specific attention heads and MLP modules involved.
Lying circuits are sparse and can be ablated to reduce deception without broadly degrading model utility.
Different types of lies (white vs. malicious, commission vs. omission) are linearly separable in activation space and controllable via distinct steering directions.
Steering vectors can increase honesty in multi-turn conversational settings, establishing a Pareto frontier between honesty and goal completion.
papers.limitation:
Analysis confined to a few model families and sizes.
Steering vectors derived from a limited set of contrastive prompts.
Multi-turn conversational setting is simplified.
Honesty steering vectors applied in the negative direction may lead to mass production of false information.
future_direction: Scaling the approach to larger models and more complex scenarios.
Investigating the transferability of steering vectors across domains.
Developing more robust safeguards against deceptive AI.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have demonstrated impressive capabilities across a variety of tasks, but their increasing autonomy in real-world applications raises concerns about their trustworthiness. While hallucinations-unintentional falsehoods-have been widely studied, the phenomenon of lying, where an LLM knowingly generates falsehoods to achieve an ulterior objective, remains underexplored. In this work, we systematically investigate the lying behavior of LLMs, differentiating it from hallucinations and testing it in practical scenarios. Through mechanistic interpretability techniques, we uncover the neural mechanisms underlying deception, employing logit lens analysis, causal interventions, and contrastive activation steering to identify and control deceptive behavior. We study real-world lying scenarios and introduce behavioral steering vectors that enable fine-grained manipulation of lying tendencies. Further, we explore the trade-offs between lying and end-task performance, establishing a Pareto frontier where dishonesty can enhance goal optimization. Our findings contribute to the broader discourse on AI ethics, shedding light on the risks and potential safeguards for deploying LLMs in high-stakes environments. Code and more illustrations are available at https://llm-liar.github.io/

papers.title: Supposedly Equivalent Facts That Aren't? Entity Frequency in Pre-training Induces Asymmetry in LLMs
papers.research_question: How does the pre-training data — the very source of an LLM’s prior knowledge — influence its propensity to hallucinate? Specifically, why does an asymmetry exist in the recognition of logically equivalent facts?
papers.core_contribution: LLMs exhibit asymmetry in recognizing logically equivalent facts, which is directly linked to frequency discrepancies of entities (as subjects vs. objects) in the pre-training data. Facts with a high-frequency subject and low-frequency object are better recognized than their inverse.
papers.conclusion: LLMs readily identify relational facts with a high-frequency subject and a low-frequency object but struggle with the inverse form, demonstrating that pre-training data characteristics (entity frequency discrepancies) shape model behavior and factual consistency.
papers.key_findings:
Facts formatted with a high-frequency subject and low-frequency object are more readily recognized than their logically equivalent inversions.
The recognition pattern flips when the frequency dynamics are reversed (low-frequency subject, high-frequency object).
No statistically significant asymmetry emerges when both entities are high-frequency.
The asymmetry persists across different model families (OLMo, Llama, Qwen) and model sizes.
The observed asymmetry is attributed to inherent biases in the pre-training data, where high-frequency entities tend to appear more often as subjects.
papers.limitation:
Focuses primarily on symmetric relations to minimize confounding factors from distinct verbalizations of non-symmetric relations.
Frequency thresholds (e.g., 100K for high-frequency, 1K for low-frequency) are empirical and may not capture the complete distribution.
future_direction: Mitigating such biases introduced by pre-training data.
Inferring characteristics of pre-training corpora, especially for models with undisclosed training data.
papers.abstract: Understanding and mitigating hallucinations in Large Language Models (LLMs) is crucial for ensuring reliable content generation. While previous research has primarily focused on "when" LLMs hallucinate, our work explains "why" and directly links model behaviour to the pre-training data that forms their prior knowledge. Specifically, we demonstrate that an asymmetry exists in the recognition of logically equivalent facts, which can be attributed to frequency discrepancies of entities appearing as subjects versus objects. Given that most pre-training datasets are inaccessible, we leverage the fully open-source OLMo series by indexing its Dolma dataset to estimate entity frequencies. Using relational facts (represented as triples) from Wikidata5M, we construct probing datasets to isolate this effect. Our experiments reveal that facts with a high-frequency subject and a low-frequency object are better recognised than their inverse, despite their logical equivalence. The pattern reverses in low-to-high frequency settings, and no statistically significant asymmetry emerges when both entities are high-frequency. These findings highlight the influential role of pre-training data in shaping model predictions and provide insights for inferring the characteristics of pre-training data in closed or partially closed LLMs.

papers.title: SAVE: Sparse Autoencoder-Driven Visual Information Enhancement for Mitigating Object Hallucination
papers.research_question: How can object hallucination in Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) be mitigated by using sparse autoencoders to identify and steer along visual understanding features?
papers.core_contribution: The paper proposes SA VE, a framework that uses sparse autoencoders to identify visual understanding features in MLLMs and steers the model along these features to mitigate object hallucination, outperforming training-free baselines.
papers.conclusion: SA VE effectively mitigates object hallucination in MLLMs by steering along visual understanding features identified via sparse autoencoders, demonstrating consistent improvements across models and benchmarks.
papers.key_findings:
SAE features can be used to identify visual understanding features that are discriminative between correct and hallucinated responses.
Steering along visual understanding features reduces object hallucination, while steering along hallucinated features amplifies it.
SA VE outperforms state-of-the-art training-free methods on CHAIR, POPE, and MMHal-Bench benchmarks.
Steering suppresses the probability of uncertain object tokens and increases attention to image tokens.
The method is robust across different MLLM architectures and layers.
papers.abstract: Although Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) have advanced substantially, they remain vulnerable to object hallucination caused by language priors and visual information loss. To address this, we propose SAVE (Sparse Autoencoder-Driven Visual Information Enhancement), a framework that mitigates hallucination by steering the model along Sparse Autoencoder (SAE) latent features. A binary object-presence question-answering probe identifies the SAE features most indicative of the model's visual information processing, referred to as visual understanding features. Steering the model along these identified features reinforces grounded visual understanding and effectively reduces hallucination. With its simple design, SAVE outperforms state-of-the-art training-free methods on standard benchmarks, achieving a 10\%p improvement in CHAIR\_S and consistent gains on POPE and MMHal-Bench. Extensive evaluations across multiple models and layers confirm the robustness and generalizability of our approach. Further analysis reveals that steering along visual understanding features suppresses the generation of uncertain object tokens and increases attention to image tokens, mitigating hallucination. Code is released at https://github.com/wiarae/SAVE.

papers.title: Treble Counterfactual VLMs: A Causal Approach to Hallucination
papers.research_question: What causes hallucination in Vision-Language Models, and how can it be mitigated using a causal perspective?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a causal framework to analyze and mitigate hallucination in VLMs by estimating Natural Direct Effects of modalities and implementing a test-time intervention to reduce unintended direct influences.
papers.conclusion: The causal framework effectively reduces modality bias and hallucination in VLMs, improving reliability while maintaining task performance.
papers.key_findings:
Our method reduces hallucination and improves accuracy on POPE and MMHal-Bench benchmarks.
Using a single PCA dimension for NDE estimation yields the best performance.
An optimal sample size of 50 for NDE estimation provides robust results.
The method is effective across random, popular, and adversarial settings.
It enhances multi-modal reasoning in attribute and comparison tasks.
papers.limitation:
The causal framework may not capture all hallucination sources, especially in open-ended tasks.
The intervention introduces inference overhead, impacting real-time use.
future_direction: Refine the causal model
Develop task-specific adaptive interventions
Integrate contrastive learning for better multi-modal alignment
papers.abstract: Vision-Language Models (VLMs) have advanced multi-modal tasks like image captioning, visual question answering, and reasoning. However, they often generate hallucinated outputs inconsistent with the visual context or prompt, limiting reliability in critical applications like autonomous driving and medical imaging. Existing studies link hallucination to statistical biases, language priors, and biased feature learning but lack a structured causal understanding. In this work, we introduce a causal perspective to analyze and mitigate hallucination in VLMs. We hypothesize that hallucination arises from unintended direct influences of either the vision or text modality, bypassing proper multi-modal fusion. To address this, we construct a causal graph for VLMs and employ counterfactual analysis to estimate the Natural Direct Effect (NDE) of vision, text, and their cross-modal interaction on the output. We systematically identify and mitigate these unintended direct effects to ensure that responses are primarily driven by genuine multi-modal fusion. Our approach consists of three steps: (1) designing structural causal graphs to distinguish correct fusion pathways from spurious modality shortcuts, (2) estimating modality-specific and cross-modal NDE using perturbed image representations, hallucinated text embeddings, and degraded visual inputs, and (3) implementing a test-time intervention module to dynamically adjust the model's dependence on each modality. Experimental results demonstrate that our method significantly reduces hallucination while preserving task performance, providing a robust and interpretable framework for improving VLM reliability. To enhance accessibility and reproducibility, our code is publicly available at https://github.com/TREE985/Treble-Counterfactual-VLMs.

papers.title: From Noise to Narrative: Tracing the Origins of Hallucinations in Transformers
papers.research_question: How do hallucinations arise in pre-trained transformer models, and how can internal concept activations predict them?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that pre-trained transformers impose semantic structure on noisy inputs, that the number of activated concepts increases with input uncertainty, and that internal concept activations can predict hallucinations in the output.
papers.conclusion: We have shown that pre-trained transformers impose coherent, steerable conceptual structure even on pure noise or randomly shuffled inputs, with the repertoire of activated concepts expanding as input structure degrades, across both images and text.
papers.key_findings:
Transformers impose semantic structure on ambiguous or noisy inputs, revealing an input-insensitive inductive bias.
The number of semantic concepts activated increases with input uncertainty, especially in middle layers.
Internal concept activations in transformer layers can reliably predict the tendency of the model to hallucinate in its output.
papers.limitation: The linear representation hypothesis may not hold for all features, and our evaluation is limited by the ImageNet dataset.
papers.abstract: As generative AI systems become competent and democratized in science, business, and government, deeper insight into their failure modes now poses an acute need. The occasional volatility in their behavior, such as the propensity of transformer models to hallucinate, impedes trust and adoption of emerging AI solutions in high-stakes areas. In the present work, we establish how and when hallucinations arise in pre-trained transformer models through concept representations captured by sparse autoencoders, under scenarios with experimentally controlled uncertainty in the input space. Our systematic experiments reveal that the number of semantic concepts used by the transformer model grows as the input information becomes increasingly unstructured. In the face of growing uncertainty in the input space, the transformer model becomes prone to activate coherent yet input-insensitive semantic features, leading to hallucinated output. At its extreme, for pure-noise inputs, we identify a wide variety of robustly triggered and meaningful concepts in the intermediate activations of pre-trained transformer models, whose functional integrity we confirm through targeted steering. We also show that hallucinations in the output of a transformer model can be reliably predicted from the concept patterns embedded in transformer layer activations. This collection of insights on transformer internal processing mechanics has immediate consequences for aligning AI models with human values, AI safety, opening the attack surface for potential adversarial attacks, and providing a basis for automatic quantification of a model's hallucination risk.

papers.title: D$^2$HScore: Reasoning-Aware Hallucination Detection via Semantic Breadth and Depth Analysis in LLMs
papers.research_question: How can hallucinations in large language models be detected by analyzing the semantic breadth and depth of internal token representations?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes D2HScore, a training-free framework for hallucination detection that jointly measures intra-layer dispersion (semantic breadth) and inter-layer drift (semantic depth) of token representations in LLMs.
papers.conclusion: D2HScore provides an effective, interpretable, and training-free approach for hallucination detection by analyzing both semantic breadth and depth in LLM internal representations, opening directions for using such scores as feedback for generation.
papers.key_findings:
D2HScore consistently outperforms existing training-free baselines across five LLMs and five benchmarks.
The Dispersion Score and Drift Score capture complementary aspects of hallucination, and their combination yields synergistic performance.
The method generalizes well to multilingual settings, as shown on the MGSM benchmark.
Attention-guided key token selection is robust and improves drift score performance over using all tokens.
Hallucinated responses exhibit lower intra-layer dispersion and weaker inter-layer drift compared to faithful ones.
papers.limitation: The method is a white-box approach requiring access to internal hidden states, so it cannot be applied to closed-source models.
future_direction: Using D2HScore as a feedback signal to guide generation and mitigate hallucinations.
papers.abstract: Although large Language Models (LLMs) have achieved remarkable success, their practical application is often hindered by the generation of non-factual content, which is called "hallucination". Ensuring the reliability of LLMs' outputs is a critical challenge, particularly in high-stakes domains such as finance, security, and healthcare. In this work, we revisit hallucination detection from the perspective of model architecture and generation dynamics. Leveraging the multi-layer structure and autoregressive decoding process of LLMs, we decompose hallucination signals into two complementary dimensions: the semantic breadth of token representations within each layer, and the semantic depth of core concepts as they evolve across layers. Based on this insight, we propose \textbf{D$^2$HScore (Dispersion and Drift-based Hallucination Score)}, a training-free and label-free framework that jointly measures: (1) \textbf{Intra-Layer Dispersion}, which quantifies the semantic diversity of token representations within each layer; and (2) \textbf{Inter-Layer Drift}, which tracks the progressive transformation of key token representations across layers. To ensure drift reflects the evolution of meaningful semantics rather than noisy or redundant tokens, we guide token selection using attention signals. By capturing both the horizontal and vertical dynamics of representation during inference, D$^2$HScore provides an interpretable and lightweight proxy for hallucination detection. Extensive experiments across five open-source LLMs and five widely used benchmarks demonstrate that D$^2$HScore consistently outperforms existing training-free baselines.

papers.title: Interpreting and Mitigating Unwanted Uncertainty in LLMs
papers.research_question: What internal mechanisms cause LLMs to flip from correct to incorrect answers under re-evaluation, and how can we intervene to mitigate this behavior?
papers.core_contribution: The paper identifies a small set of non-retrieval attention heads that cause unwanted uncertainty in LLMs and shows that targeted masking of these heads reduces flip behavior by up to 15% without harming baseline accuracy.
papers.conclusion: Unwanted uncertainty in LLMs is not a byproduct of retrieval failure, but rather a consequence of specific attention heads that influence decision-making under re-evaluation; masking these heads can reduce flip behavior while preserving overall accuracy.
papers.key_findings:
Retrieval heads are not primarily responsible for avoiding uncertainty.
A small set of non-retrieval attention heads disproportionately attend to misleading tokens in uncertain contexts.
Masking these heads reduces flip behavior by up to 15% without introducing incoherence or overcorrection.
Masking uncertainty heads is effective only in cases of low uncertainty and can lead to overconfidence in incorrect answers in high-uncertainty tasks.
There exist some non-retrieval heads responsible for coherent outputs.
papers.limitation: Masking uncertainty heads can increase overconfidence in incorrect predictions in high-uncertainty tasks.
future_direction: Generalization to other models, architectures, and tasks.
Identifying and characterizing heads that yield incoherent outputs.
Better uncertainty head detection by analyzing attention head output vectors.
papers.abstract: Despite their impressive capabilities, Large Language Models (LLMs) exhibit unwanted uncertainty, a phenomenon where a model changes a previously correct answer into an incorrect one when re-prompted. This behavior undermines trust and poses serious risks in high-stakes domains. In this work, we investigate the mechanisms that drive this phenomenon. We adapt the Needle-in-a-Haystack retrieval framework and integrate a Flip-style re-evaluation prompt to simulate realistic answer-flipping scenarios. We find that retrieval heads are not primarily responsible for avoiding uncertainty. Instead, we identify a small set of non-retrieval attention heads that disproportionately attend to misleading tokens in uncertain contexts. Masking these heads yields significant improvements, reducing flip behavior by up to 15% without introducing incoherence or overcorrection. However, when tested for downstream tasks, we observe trade-offs with flip behavior. Our findings contribute to the growing field of mechanistic interpretability and present a simple yet effective technique for mitigating uncertainty-driven failure modes in LLMs.

papers.title: SAKED: Mitigating Hallucination in Large Vision-Language Models via Stability-Aware Knowledge Enhanced Decoding
papers.research_question: How does instability in a model's internal knowledge contribute to hallucinations in Large Vision-Language Models?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes SAKED, a training-free decoding method that uses a layer-wise Knowledge Stability Score (KSS) to quantify and leverage stable internal knowledge, thereby mitigating hallucinations in LVLMs without additional training.
papers.conclusion: SAKED effectively mitigates hallucinations by dynamically leveraging stable internal knowledge, providing a practical step toward safer and more reliable multimodal generation.
papers.key_findings:
Visual activation drift across attention heads is associated with hallucinations.
Large knowledge fluctuations across model layers correlate with higher hallucination risk.
Substantial distraction in visual focus between neighboring output tokens increases the likelihood of hallucinations.
SAKED achieves state-of-the-art hallucination mitigation performance across multiple models and benchmarks.
SAKED is a plug-and-play method that does not require model fine-tuning.
papers.limitation: In early generation stages with short sequences, the Cross-Token Stability Score (CTSS) has limited impact because temporal dependencies are less pronounced.
future_direction: Investigate more flexible ways to leverage CHSS, CLSS, and CTSS throughout the generation process with adaptive weighting.
Explore using CHSS, CLSS, and CTSS as auxiliary supervision signals during training to encourage models to suppress hallucination-prone behaviors.
papers.abstract: Hallucinations in Large Vision-Language Models (LVLMs) pose significant security and reliability risks in real-world applications. Inspired by the observation that humans are more error-prone when uncertain or hesitant, we investigate how instability in a model 's internal knowledge contributes to LVLM hallucinations. We conduct extensive empirical analyses from three perspectives, namely attention heads, model layers, and decoding tokens, and identify three key hallucination patterns: (i) visual activation drift across attention heads, (ii) pronounced knowledge fluctuations across layers, and (iii) visual focus distraction between neighboring output tokens. Building on these findings, we propose Stability-Aware Knowledge-Enhanced Decoding (SAKED), which introduces a layer-wise Knowledge Stability Score (KSS) to quantify knowledge stability throughout the model. By contrasting the most stability-aware and stability-agnostic layers, SAKED suppresses decoding noise and dynamically leverages the most reliable internal knowledge for faithful token generation. Moreover, SAKED is training-free and can be seamlessly integrated into different architectures. Extensive experiments demonstrate that SAKED achieves state-of-the-art performance for hallucination mitigation on various models, tasks, and benchmarks.

papers.title: Seeing It or Not? Interpretable Vision-aware Latent Steering to Mitigate Object Hallucinations
papers.research_question: How do visual inputs influence the decision-making processes of Large Vision-Language Models, and how can we use this understanding to mitigate object hallucinations?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces VaLSe, a vision-aware latent steering framework that uses interpretable visual contribution maps to trace visual influence on token generation and then steers internal representations to mitigate object hallucinations in LVLMs.
papers.conclusion: VaLSe effectively mitigates object hallucinations and provides interpretable insights into model decision-making, while also revealing limitations in current OH benchmarks and advocating for more nuanced evaluation.
papers.key_findings:
VaLSe reduces object hallucination metrics (CS, CI) on multiple benchmarks while preserving general task performance.
Visual contribution maps show that models may generate correct answers while attending to irrelevant image regions, indicating reliance on language priors.
Existing OH metrics like CHAIR sometimes flag visually grounded and accurate descriptions as hallucinations, indicating limitations in current evaluation.
The method can identify potential reasons for hallucinations, such as attention to misleading visual cues (e.g., logos leading to 'cell phone' hallucination).
Latent steering using SVD-derived directions effectively shifts model focus to semantically relevant image content.
papers.limitation:
VaLSe is less effective on models with complex vision encoders like Qwen2-VL due to difficulty in tracing visual token influence.
Limited improvement on multiple-choice question formats (e.g., MMVP benchmark).
future_direction: Developing more nuanced, interpretable, and visually grounded benchmarks for object hallucination evaluation.
Incorporating interpretability more critically in future hallucination mitigation research.
papers.abstract: Large Vision-Language Models (LVLMs) have achieved remarkable success but continue to struggle with object hallucination (OH), generating outputs inconsistent with visual inputs. While previous work has proposed methods to reduce OH, the visual decision-making mechanisms that lead to hallucinations remain poorly understood. In this paper, we propose VaLSe, a Vision-aware Latent Steering framework that adopts an interpretation-then-mitigation strategy to address OH in LVLMs. By tackling dual challenges of modeling complex vision-language interactions and eliminating spurious activation artifacts, VaLSe can generate visual contribution maps that trace how specific visual inputs influence individual output tokens. These maps reveal the model's vision-aware focus regions, which are then used to perform latent space steering, realigning internal representations toward semantically relevant content and reducing hallucinated outputs. Extensive experiments demonstrate that VaLSe is a powerful interpretability tool and an effective method for enhancing model robustness against OH across multiple benchmarks. Furthermore, our analysis uncovers limitations in existing OH evaluation metrics, underscoring the need for more nuanced, interpretable, and visually grounded OH benchmarks in future work. Code is available at: https://github.com/Ziwei-Zheng/VaLSe.

papers.title: TPA: Next Token Probability Attribution for Detecting Hallucinations in RAG
papers.research_question: Is the binary conflict between FFNs and RAG the only cause of hallucination? Do contributions from other components like LayerNorm and User Query also drive hallucinations?
papers.core_contribution: TPA is a novel framework that mathematically attributes each token's probability to seven distinct sources (Query, RAG Context, Past Token, Self Token, FFN, Final LayerNorm, Initial Embedding) and uses syntax-aware aggregation to detect hallucinations in RAG, achieving state-of-the-art performance.
papers.conclusion: TPA effectively detects RAG hallucinations by attributing token probability to seven sources and using syntax-aware features, outperforming baselines and showing that hallucination signals vary across models, necessitating a learnable approach.
papers.key_findings:
TPA achieves state-of-the-art hallucination detection performance across diverse LLM architectures (Llama2, Llama3, Mistral, Qwen3).
Fine-grained attribution beyond the binary FFN-RAG conflict is necessary for robust detection; previously overlooked sources like LayerNorm are vital.
Syntactic aggregation (by POS tags) captures model-specific grounding logic, enabling the detector to pinpoint anomalies in specific entities.
Hallucination fingerprints vary across model architectures, confirming the need for a learnable approach rather than static heuristics.
The method provides transparent interpretability, automatically uncovering novel mechanistic signatures such as anomalous LayerNorm contributions.
papers.limitation:
Relies on white-box access to model internals, preventing application to closed-source APIs.
The decomposition incurs higher computational overhead than simple scalar probes.
Feature engineering depends on external linguistic tools (POS taggers), which may limit generalization to specialized domains like code generation.
future_direction: Extending TPA to phrase- or span-level attribution for efficiency.
Active mitigation via online monitoring and intervention on risky patterns (e.g., abnormal FFN or LN reliance).
Studying TPA under noisy or adversarial retrieval, where expected source shifts may themselves serve as detection signals.
Extending POS-based aggregation to non-English and specialized domains (code, scientific text) via multilingual spaCy or AST node types.
papers.abstract: Detecting hallucinations in Retrieval-Augmented Generation remains a challenge. Prior approaches attribute hallucinations to a binary conflict between internal knowledge stored in FFNs and the retrieved context. However, this perspective is incomplete, failing to account for the impact of other components of the LLM, such as the user query, previously generated tokens, the self token, and the final LayerNorm adjustment. To comprehensively capture the impact of these components on hallucination detection, we propose TPA which mathematically attributes each token's probability to seven distinct sources: Query, RAG Context, Past Token, Self Token, FFN, Final LayerNorm, and Initial Embedding. This attribution quantifies how each source contributes to the generation of the next token. Specifically, we aggregate these attribution scores by Part-of-Speech (POS) tags to quantify the contribution of each model component to the generation of specific linguistic categories within a response. By leveraging these patterns, such as detecting anomalies where Nouns rely heavily on LayerNorm, TPA effectively identifies hallucinated responses. Extensive experiments show that TPA achieves state-of-the-art performance.

papers.title: Beyond Logit Lens: Contextual Embeddings for Robust Hallucination Detection & Grounding in VLMs
papers.research_question: What are the limitations of the logit lens for hallucination detection in VLMs, and how can contextual embeddings from middle layers improve detection and grounding?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces ContextualLens, a training-free method that uses contextual embeddings from middle layers of VLMs to improve hallucination detection and grounding, overcoming limitations of the logit lens.
papers.conclusion: ContextualLens leverages contextual embeddings to enhance hallucination detection and grounding in VLMs, providing a reliable and interpretable method without requiring training.
papers.key_findings:
ContextualLens significantly improves hallucination detection in categories like attributes, comparisons, and relations where logit lens performs poorly.
The method enables transition from zero-shot object segmentation to grounded visual question answering with precise bounding boxes.
Contextual embeddings from middle layers are more effective for multi-token concepts and contextual understanding.
papers.limitation:
Validation conducted primarily on factual short answer VQA datasets, limiting generalization to more diverse and complex datasets.
ContextualLens is outperformed by output probabilities in the Count category.
While precise, the bounding box method has lower recall, indicating room for improvement in evidence coverage.
future_direction: Extending validation to more diverse and complex datasets beyond factual short answer VQA.
Exploring extensions to the method for abstractive scenarios such as counting.
Improving recall by leveraging scoring mechanisms as priors for pre-trained segmentation models or enhancing evaluation metrics.
papers.abstract: The rapid development of Large Multimodal Models (LMMs) has significantly advanced multimodal understanding by harnessing the language abilities of Large Language Models (LLMs) and integrating modality-specific encoders. However, LMMs are plagued by hallucinations that limit their reliability and adoption. While traditional methods to detect and mitigate these hallucinations often involve costly training or rely heavily on external models, recent approaches utilizing internal model features present a promising alternative. In this paper, we critically assess the limitations of the state-of-the-art training-free technique, the logit lens, in handling generalized visual hallucinations. We introduce ContextualLens, a refined method that leverages contextual token embeddings from middle layers of LMMs. This approach significantly improves hallucination detection and grounding across diverse categories, including actions and OCR, while also excelling in tasks requiring contextual understanding, such as spatial relations and attribute comparison. Our novel grounding technique yields highly precise bounding boxes, facilitating a transition from Zero-Shot Object Segmentation to Grounded Visual Question Answering. Our contributions pave the way for more reliable and interpretable multimodal models.

papers.title: Weakly Supervised Detection of Hallucinations in LLM Activations
papers.research_question: This paper investigates whether pre-trained LLMs encode hallucination patterns in their internal states and proposes a weakly supervised method to detect such patterns without prior knowledge of the anomaly type.
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces a weakly supervised auditing method that uses subset scanning to detect hallucination patterns in LLM activations without requiring labeled anomalous data, achieving performance similar to a supervised classifier.
papers.conclusion: The proposed weakly supervised auditing method can detect hallucinations in LLM activations without needing labeled anomalous data, performing similarly to a supervised baseline, and the identified nodes could be used for targeted fine-tuning.
papers.key_findings:
BERT shows limited internal capacity for encoding hallucinations, while OPT encodes hallucination information effectively.
The weakly supervised scanning method performs comparably to a supervised classifier in detecting hallucinations.
The method can detect anomalies (hallucinations, toxicity, stereotypes) without prior knowledge of the anomaly type.
The method identifies subsets of nodes that are pivotal for encoding anomalous patterns.
The method's performance varies with the amount of anomalous data in the test set.
papers.limitation:
Assumes the reference dataset contains only normal statements, which may not be realistic.
Only has positive predictive ability; cannot confirm the absence of anomalies.
future_direction: Extend the method to reference datasets that contain small amounts of anomalous data or are composed of various data sources.
Use the identified pivotal nodes to guide fine-tuning of sub-networks for bias mitigation.
papers.abstract: We propose an auditing method to identify whether a large language model (LLM) encodes patterns such as hallucinations in its internal states, which may propagate to downstream tasks. We introduce a weakly supervised auditing technique using a subset scanning approach to detect anomalous patterns in LLM activations from pre-trained models. Importantly, our method does not need knowledge of the type of patterns a-priori. Instead, it relies on a reference dataset devoid of anomalies during testing. Further, our approach enables the identification of pivotal nodes responsible for encoding these patterns, which may offer crucial insights for fine-tuning specific sub-networks for bias mitigation. We introduce two new scanning methods to handle LLM activations for anomalous sentences that may deviate from the expected distribution in either direction. Our results confirm prior findings of BERT's limited internal capacity for encoding hallucinations, while OPT appears capable of encoding hallucination information internally. Importantly, our scanning approach, without prior exposure to false statements, performs comparably to a fully supervised out-of-distribution classifier.

papers.title: Exploring Causes and Mitigation of Hallucinations in Large Vision Language Models
papers.research_question: What are the causes of hallucinations in Large Vision Language Models during image captioning, and how can they be mitigated?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces a method to detect and reduce hallucinations in LVLMs by comparing token-level hidden representations from inference passes with and without the image, training a classifier on this difference, and using it to guide a novel decoding strategy.
papers.conclusion: Hallucinations in LVLMs arise as language priors override visual information during generation; the proposed method using hidden state differences effectively reduces these hallucinations.
papers.key_findings:
Hallucinations are more likely to occur in the later parts of generated captions.
LVLMs show inconsistent object recognition between generative and discriminative tasks.
Token probability distributions are highly similar with and without image input, indicating heavy reliance on language priors.
A classifier trained on the difference between hidden states with and without the image can effectively predict token-level hallucinations.
The proposed decoding strategy using this classifier significantly reduces hallucination rates in image captioning.
papers.limitation:
The approach may penalize cases where the description of visual content naturally aligns with statistical patterns learned from training data.
The implementation uses basic vector subtraction without exploring more sophisticated distance metrics.
The classifier is highly model-specific and task-dependent, limiting its applicability to other models or tasks.
The token-level classifier was trained with sentence-level annotations, reducing its ability to make fine-grained judgments about hallucinated content.
future_direction: Developing generalized end-to-end solutions to address hallucinations in LVLMs beyond image captioning.
papers.abstract: Large Vision-Language Models (LVLMs) integrate image encoders with Large Language Models (LLMs) to process multi-modal inputs and perform complex visual tasks. However, they often generate hallucinations by describing non-existent objects or attributes, compromising their reliability. This study analyzes hallucination patterns in image captioning, showing that not all tokens in the generation process are influenced by image input and that image dependency can serve as a useful signal for hallucination detection. To address this, we develop an automated pipeline to identify hallucinated objects and train a token-level classifier using hidden representations from parallel inference passes-with and without image input. Leveraging this classifier, we introduce a decoding strategy that effectively controls hallucination rates in image captioning at inference time.

papers.title: Cross-Layer Attention Probing for Fine-Grained Hallucination Detection
papers.research_question: How can we improve hallucination detection in LLMs by probing activations across the entire residual stream?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Cross-Layer Attention Probing (CLAP), a novel probing technique that uses attention over the residual stream to improve hallucination detection in LLMs, enabling fine-grained detection and integration with mitigation strategies.
papers.conclusion: CLAP is an effective method for detecting and mitigating hallucinations in LLMs by leveraging cross-layer attention over the residual stream, outperforming existing approaches and generalizing well out-of-distribution.
papers.key_findings:
CLAP improves hallucination detection over uncertainty baselines and single-layer probes on multiple LLMs and tasks.
CLAP enables fine-grained detection of hallucinations among sampled responses to the same prompt.
Combining CLAP with mitigation strategies like DoLa reduces hallucination rates while minimizing negative impacts on non-hallucinated responses.
CLAP generalizes better out-of-distribution compared to layer-specific probes and semantic entropy probes.
Ablation studies show that cross-layer attention is crucial for CLAP's performance and generalizability.
papers.limitation:
Focused on small LLMs (2B-8B parameters), leaving scaling to larger LLMs for future work.
The role of each layer within CLAP is not investigated and left for future work.
future_direction: Scaling CLAP to larger LLMs
Investigating the role of each layer within CLAP
papers.abstract: With the large-scale adoption of Large Language Models (LLMs) in various applications, there is a growing reliability concern due to their tendency to generate inaccurate text, i.e. hallucinations. In this work, we propose Cross-Layer Attention Probing (CLAP), a novel activation probing technique for hallucination detection, which processes the LLM activations across the entire residual stream as a joint sequence. Our empirical evaluations using five LLMs and three tasks show that CLAP improves hallucination detection compared to baselines on both greedy decoded responses as well as responses sampled at higher temperatures, thus enabling fine-grained detection, i.e. the ability to disambiguate hallucinations and non-hallucinations among different sampled responses to a given prompt. This allows us to propose a detect-then-mitigate strategy using CLAP to reduce hallucinations and improve LLM reliability compared to direct mitigation approaches. Finally, we show that CLAP maintains high reliability even when applied out-of-distribution.

papers.title: Interpreting and Editing Vision-Language Representations to Mitigate Hallucinations
papers.research_question: How can we interpret and edit the internal image representations of vision-language models to detect and reduce object hallucinations?
