papers.core_contribution: Introduces a causal framework to analyze and mitigate hallucination in VLMs by estimating Natural Direct Effects of modalities and implementing a test-time intervention to reduce unintended direct influences.
papers.conclusion: The causal framework effectively reduces modality bias and hallucination in VLMs, improving reliability while maintaining task performance.
papers.key_findings:
Our method reduces hallucination and improves accuracy on POPE and MMHal-Bench benchmarks.
Using a single PCA dimension for NDE estimation yields the best performance.
An optimal sample size of 50 for NDE estimation provides robust results.
The method is effective across random, popular, and adversarial settings.
It enhances multi-modal reasoning in attribute and comparison tasks.
papers.limitation:
The causal framework may not capture all hallucination sources, especially in open-ended tasks.
The intervention introduces inference overhead, impacting real-time use.
future_direction: Refine the causal model
Develop task-specific adaptive interventions
Integrate contrastive learning for better multi-modal alignment
papers.abstract: Vision-Language Models (VLMs) have advanced multi-modal tasks like image captioning, visual question answering, and reasoning. However, they often generate hallucinated outputs inconsistent with the visual context or prompt, limiting reliability in critical applications like autonomous driving and medical imaging. Existing studies link hallucination to statistical biases, language priors, and biased feature learning but lack a structured causal understanding. In this work, we introduce a causal perspective to analyze and mitigate hallucination in VLMs. We hypothesize that hallucination arises from unintended direct influences of either the vision or text modality, bypassing proper multi-modal fusion. To address this, we construct a causal graph for VLMs and employ counterfactual analysis to estimate the Natural Direct Effect (NDE) of vision, text, and their cross-modal interaction on the output. We systematically identify and mitigate these unintended direct effects to ensure that responses are primarily driven by genuine multi-modal fusion. Our approach consists of three steps: (1) designing structural causal graphs to distinguish correct fusion pathways from spurious modality shortcuts, (2) estimating modality-specific and cross-modal NDE using perturbed image representations, hallucinated text embeddings, and degraded visual inputs, and (3) implementing a test-time intervention module to dynamically adjust the model's dependence on each modality. Experimental results demonstrate that our method significantly reduces hallucination while preserving task performance, providing a robust and interpretable framework for improving VLM reliability. To enhance accessibility and reproducibility, our code is publicly available at https://github.com/TREE985/Treble-Counterfactual-VLMs.

papers.title: From Noise to Narrative: Tracing the Origins of Hallucinations in Transformers
papers.research_question: How do hallucinations arise in pre-trained transformer models, and how can internal concept activations predict them?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that pre-trained transformers impose semantic structure on noisy inputs, that the number of activated concepts increases with input uncertainty, and that internal concept activations can predict hallucinations in the output.
papers.conclusion: We have shown that pre-trained transformers impose coherent, steerable conceptual structure even on pure noise or randomly shuffled inputs, with the repertoire of activated concepts expanding as input structure degrades, across both images and text.
papers.key_findings:
Transformers impose semantic structure on ambiguous or noisy inputs, revealing an input-insensitive inductive bias.
The number of semantic concepts activated increases with input uncertainty, especially in middle layers.
Internal concept activations in transformer layers can reliably predict the tendency of the model to hallucinate in its output.
papers.limitation: The linear representation hypothesis may not hold for all features, and our evaluation is limited by the ImageNet dataset.
papers.abstract: As generative AI systems become competent and democratized in science, business, and government, deeper insight into their failure modes now poses an acute need. The occasional volatility in their behavior, such as the propensity of transformer models to hallucinate, impedes trust and adoption of emerging AI solutions in high-stakes areas. In the present work, we establish how and when hallucinations arise in pre-trained transformer models through concept representations captured by sparse autoencoders, under scenarios with experimentally controlled uncertainty in the input space. Our systematic experiments reveal that the number of semantic concepts used by the transformer model grows as the input information becomes increasingly unstructured. In the face of growing uncertainty in the input space, the transformer model becomes prone to activate coherent yet input-insensitive semantic features, leading to hallucinated output. At its extreme, for pure-noise inputs, we identify a wide variety of robustly triggered and meaningful concepts in the intermediate activations of pre-trained transformer models, whose functional integrity we confirm through targeted steering. We also show that hallucinations in the output of a transformer model can be reliably predicted from the concept patterns embedded in transformer layer activations. This collection of insights on transformer internal processing mechanics has immediate consequences for aligning AI models with human values, AI safety, opening the attack surface for potential adversarial attacks, and providing a basis for automatic quantification of a model's hallucination risk.

papers.title: D$^2$HScore: Reasoning-Aware Hallucination Detection via Semantic Breadth and Depth Analysis in LLMs
papers.research_question: How can hallucinations in large language models be detected by analyzing the semantic breadth and depth of internal token representations?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes D2HScore, a training-free framework for hallucination detection that jointly measures intra-layer dispersion (semantic breadth) and inter-layer drift (semantic depth) of token representations in LLMs.
papers.conclusion: D2HScore provides an effective, interpretable, and training-free approach for hallucination detection by analyzing both semantic breadth and depth in LLM internal representations, opening directions for using such scores as feedback for generation.
papers.key_findings:
D2HScore consistently outperforms existing training-free baselines across five LLMs and five benchmarks.
The Dispersion Score and Drift Score capture complementary aspects of hallucination, and their combination yields synergistic performance.
The method generalizes well to multilingual settings, as shown on the MGSM benchmark.
Attention-guided key token selection is robust and improves drift score performance over using all tokens.
Hallucinated responses exhibit lower intra-layer dispersion and weaker inter-layer drift compared to faithful ones.
papers.limitation: The method is a white-box approach requiring access to internal hidden states, so it cannot be applied to closed-source models.
future_direction: Using D2HScore as a feedback signal to guide generation and mitigate hallucinations.
papers.abstract: Although large Language Models (LLMs) have achieved remarkable success, their practical application is often hindered by the generation of non-factual content, which is called "hallucination". Ensuring the reliability of LLMs' outputs is a critical challenge, particularly in high-stakes domains such as finance, security, and healthcare. In this work, we revisit hallucination detection from the perspective of model architecture and generation dynamics. Leveraging the multi-layer structure and autoregressive decoding process of LLMs, we decompose hallucination signals into two complementary dimensions: the semantic breadth of token representations within each layer, and the semantic depth of core concepts as they evolve across layers. Based on this insight, we propose \textbf{D$^2$HScore (Dispersion and Drift-based Hallucination Score)}, a training-free and label-free framework that jointly measures: (1) \textbf{Intra-Layer Dispersion}, which quantifies the semantic diversity of token representations within each layer; and (2) \textbf{Inter-Layer Drift}, which tracks the progressive transformation of key token representations across layers. To ensure drift reflects the evolution of meaningful semantics rather than noisy or redundant tokens, we guide token selection using attention signals. By capturing both the horizontal and vertical dynamics of representation during inference, D$^2$HScore provides an interpretable and lightweight proxy for hallucination detection. Extensive experiments across five open-source LLMs and five widely used benchmarks demonstrate that D$^2$HScore consistently outperforms existing training-free baselines.

papers.title: Interpreting and Mitigating Unwanted Uncertainty in LLMs
papers.research_question: What internal mechanisms cause LLMs to flip from correct to incorrect answers under re-evaluation, and how can we intervene to mitigate this behavior?
papers.core_contribution: The paper identifies a small set of non-retrieval attention heads that cause unwanted uncertainty in LLMs and shows that targeted masking of these heads reduces flip behavior by up to 15% without harming baseline accuracy.
papers.conclusion: Unwanted uncertainty in LLMs is not a byproduct of retrieval failure, but rather a consequence of specific attention heads that influence decision-making under re-evaluation; masking these heads can reduce flip behavior while preserving overall accuracy.
papers.key_findings:
Retrieval heads are not primarily responsible for avoiding uncertainty.
A small set of non-retrieval attention heads disproportionately attend to misleading tokens in uncertain contexts.
Masking these heads reduces flip behavior by up to 15% without introducing incoherence or overcorrection.
Masking uncertainty heads is effective only in cases of low uncertainty and can lead to overconfidence in incorrect answers in high-uncertainty tasks.
There exist some non-retrieval heads responsible for coherent outputs.
papers.limitation: Masking uncertainty heads can increase overconfidence in incorrect predictions in high-uncertainty tasks.
future_direction: Generalization to other models, architectures, and tasks.
Identifying and characterizing heads that yield incoherent outputs.
Better uncertainty head detection by analyzing attention head output vectors.
papers.abstract: Despite their impressive capabilities, Large Language Models (LLMs) exhibit unwanted uncertainty, a phenomenon where a model changes a previously correct answer into an incorrect one when re-prompted. This behavior undermines trust and poses serious risks in high-stakes domains. In this work, we investigate the mechanisms that drive this phenomenon. We adapt the Needle-in-a-Haystack retrieval framework and integrate a Flip-style re-evaluation prompt to simulate realistic answer-flipping scenarios. We find that retrieval heads are not primarily responsible for avoiding uncertainty. Instead, we identify a small set of non-retrieval attention heads that disproportionately attend to misleading tokens in uncertain contexts. Masking these heads yields significant improvements, reducing flip behavior by up to 15% without introducing incoherence or overcorrection. However, when tested for downstream tasks, we observe trade-offs with flip behavior. Our findings contribute to the growing field of mechanistic interpretability and present a simple yet effective technique for mitigating uncertainty-driven failure modes in LLMs.

papers.title: SAKED: Mitigating Hallucination in Large Vision-Language Models via Stability-Aware Knowledge Enhanced Decoding
papers.research_question: How does instability in a model's internal knowledge contribute to hallucinations in Large Vision-Language Models?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes SAKED, a training-free decoding method that uses a layer-wise Knowledge Stability Score (KSS) to quantify and leverage stable internal knowledge, thereby mitigating hallucinations in LVLMs without additional training.
papers.conclusion: SAKED effectively mitigates hallucinations by dynamically leveraging stable internal knowledge, providing a practical step toward safer and more reliable multimodal generation.
papers.key_findings:
Visual activation drift across attention heads is associated with hallucinations.
Large knowledge fluctuations across model layers correlate with higher hallucination risk.
Substantial distraction in visual focus between neighboring output tokens increases the likelihood of hallucinations.
SAKED achieves state-of-the-art hallucination mitigation performance across multiple models and benchmarks.
SAKED is a plug-and-play method that does not require model fine-tuning.
papers.limitation: In early generation stages with short sequences, the Cross-Token Stability Score (CTSS) has limited impact because temporal dependencies are less pronounced.
future_direction: Investigate more flexible ways to leverage CHSS, CLSS, and CTSS throughout the generation process with adaptive weighting.
Explore using CHSS, CLSS, and CTSS as auxiliary supervision signals during training to encourage models to suppress hallucination-prone behaviors.
papers.abstract: Hallucinations in Large Vision-Language Models (LVLMs) pose significant security and reliability risks in real-world applications. Inspired by the observation that humans are more error-prone when uncertain or hesitant, we investigate how instability in a model 's internal knowledge contributes to LVLM hallucinations. We conduct extensive empirical analyses from three perspectives, namely attention heads, model layers, and decoding tokens, and identify three key hallucination patterns: (i) visual activation drift across attention heads, (ii) pronounced knowledge fluctuations across layers, and (iii) visual focus distraction between neighboring output tokens. Building on these findings, we propose Stability-Aware Knowledge-Enhanced Decoding (SAKED), which introduces a layer-wise Knowledge Stability Score (KSS) to quantify knowledge stability throughout the model. By contrasting the most stability-aware and stability-agnostic layers, SAKED suppresses decoding noise and dynamically leverages the most reliable internal knowledge for faithful token generation. Moreover, SAKED is training-free and can be seamlessly integrated into different architectures. Extensive experiments demonstrate that SAKED achieves state-of-the-art performance for hallucination mitigation on various models, tasks, and benchmarks.

papers.title: Seeing It or Not? Interpretable Vision-aware Latent Steering to Mitigate Object Hallucinations
papers.research_question: How do visual inputs influence the decision-making processes of Large Vision-Language Models, and how can we use this understanding to mitigate object hallucinations?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces VaLSe, a vision-aware latent steering framework that uses interpretable visual contribution maps to trace visual influence on token generation and then steers internal representations to mitigate object hallucinations in LVLMs.
papers.conclusion: VaLSe effectively mitigates object hallucinations and provides interpretable insights into model decision-making, while also revealing limitations in current OH benchmarks and advocating for more nuanced evaluation.
papers.key_findings:
VaLSe reduces object hallucination metrics (CS, CI) on multiple benchmarks while preserving general task performance.
Visual contribution maps show that models may generate correct answers while attending to irrelevant image regions, indicating reliance on language priors.
Existing OH metrics like CHAIR sometimes flag visually grounded and accurate descriptions as hallucinations, indicating limitations in current evaluation.
The method can identify potential reasons for hallucinations, such as attention to misleading visual cues (e.g., logos leading to 'cell phone' hallucination).
Latent steering using SVD-derived directions effectively shifts model focus to semantically relevant image content.
papers.limitation:
VaLSe is less effective on models with complex vision encoders like Qwen2-VL due to difficulty in tracing visual token influence.
Limited improvement on multiple-choice question formats (e.g., MMVP benchmark).
future_direction: Developing more nuanced, interpretable, and visually grounded benchmarks for object hallucination evaluation.
Incorporating interpretability more critically in future hallucination mitigation research.
papers.abstract: Large Vision-Language Models (LVLMs) have achieved remarkable success but continue to struggle with object hallucination (OH), generating outputs inconsistent with visual inputs. While previous work has proposed methods to reduce OH, the visual decision-making mechanisms that lead to hallucinations remain poorly understood. In this paper, we propose VaLSe, a Vision-aware Latent Steering framework that adopts an interpretation-then-mitigation strategy to address OH in LVLMs. By tackling dual challenges of modeling complex vision-language interactions and eliminating spurious activation artifacts, VaLSe can generate visual contribution maps that trace how specific visual inputs influence individual output tokens. These maps reveal the model's vision-aware focus regions, which are then used to perform latent space steering, realigning internal representations toward semantically relevant content and reducing hallucinated outputs. Extensive experiments demonstrate that VaLSe is a powerful interpretability tool and an effective method for enhancing model robustness against OH across multiple benchmarks. Furthermore, our analysis uncovers limitations in existing OH evaluation metrics, underscoring the need for more nuanced, interpretable, and visually grounded OH benchmarks in future work. Code is available at: https://github.com/Ziwei-Zheng/VaLSe.

papers.title: TPA: Next Token Probability Attribution for Detecting Hallucinations in RAG
papers.research_question: Is the binary conflict between FFNs and RAG the only cause of hallucination? Do contributions from other components like LayerNorm and User Query also drive hallucinations?
papers.core_contribution: TPA is a novel framework that mathematically attributes each token's probability to seven distinct sources (Query, RAG Context, Past Token, Self Token, FFN, Final LayerNorm, Initial Embedding) and uses syntax-aware aggregation to detect hallucinations in RAG, achieving state-of-the-art performance.
papers.conclusion: TPA effectively detects RAG hallucinations by attributing token probability to seven sources and using syntax-aware features, outperforming baselines and showing that hallucination signals vary across models, necessitating a learnable approach.
papers.key_findings:
TPA achieves state-of-the-art hallucination detection performance across diverse LLM architectures (Llama2, Llama3, Mistral, Qwen3).
Fine-grained attribution beyond the binary FFN-RAG conflict is necessary for robust detection; previously overlooked sources like LayerNorm are vital.
Syntactic aggregation (by POS tags) captures model-specific grounding logic, enabling the detector to pinpoint anomalies in specific entities.
Hallucination fingerprints vary across model architectures, confirming the need for a learnable approach rather than static heuristics.
The method provides transparent interpretability, automatically uncovering novel mechanistic signatures such as anomalous LayerNorm contributions.
papers.limitation:
Relies on white-box access to model internals, preventing application to closed-source APIs.
The decomposition incurs higher computational overhead than simple scalar probes.
Feature engineering depends on external linguistic tools (POS taggers), which may limit generalization to specialized domains like code generation.
future_direction: Extending TPA to phrase- or span-level attribution for efficiency.
Active mitigation via online monitoring and intervention on risky patterns (e.g., abnormal FFN or LN reliance).
Studying TPA under noisy or adversarial retrieval, where expected source shifts may themselves serve as detection signals.
Extending POS-based aggregation to non-English and specialized domains (code, scientific text) via multilingual spaCy or AST node types.
papers.abstract: Detecting hallucinations in Retrieval-Augmented Generation remains a challenge. Prior approaches attribute hallucinations to a binary conflict between internal knowledge stored in FFNs and the retrieved context. However, this perspective is incomplete, failing to account for the impact of other components of the LLM, such as the user query, previously generated tokens, the self token, and the final LayerNorm adjustment. To comprehensively capture the impact of these components on hallucination detection, we propose TPA which mathematically attributes each token's probability to seven distinct sources: Query, RAG Context, Past Token, Self Token, FFN, Final LayerNorm, and Initial Embedding. This attribution quantifies how each source contributes to the generation of the next token. Specifically, we aggregate these attribution scores by Part-of-Speech (POS) tags to quantify the contribution of each model component to the generation of specific linguistic categories within a response. By leveraging these patterns, such as detecting anomalies where Nouns rely heavily on LayerNorm, TPA effectively identifies hallucinated responses. Extensive experiments show that TPA achieves state-of-the-art performance.

papers.title: Beyond Logit Lens: Contextual Embeddings for Robust Hallucination Detection & Grounding in VLMs
papers.research_question: What are the limitations of the logit lens for hallucination detection in VLMs, and how can contextual embeddings from middle layers improve detection and grounding?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces ContextualLens, a training-free method that uses contextual embeddings from middle layers of VLMs to improve hallucination detection and grounding, overcoming limitations of the logit lens.
papers.conclusion: ContextualLens leverages contextual embeddings to enhance hallucination detection and grounding in VLMs, providing a reliable and interpretable method without requiring training.
papers.key_findings:
ContextualLens significantly improves hallucination detection in categories like attributes, comparisons, and relations where logit lens performs poorly.
The method enables transition from zero-shot object segmentation to grounded visual question answering with precise bounding boxes.
Contextual embeddings from middle layers are more effective for multi-token concepts and contextual understanding.
papers.limitation:
Validation conducted primarily on factual short answer VQA datasets, limiting generalization to more diverse and complex datasets.
ContextualLens is outperformed by output probabilities in the Count category.
While precise, the bounding box method has lower recall, indicating room for improvement in evidence coverage.
future_direction: Extending validation to more diverse and complex datasets beyond factual short answer VQA.
Exploring extensions to the method for abstractive scenarios such as counting.
Improving recall by leveraging scoring mechanisms as priors for pre-trained segmentation models or enhancing evaluation metrics.
papers.abstract: The rapid development of Large Multimodal Models (LMMs) has significantly advanced multimodal understanding by harnessing the language abilities of Large Language Models (LLMs) and integrating modality-specific encoders. However, LMMs are plagued by hallucinations that limit their reliability and adoption. While traditional methods to detect and mitigate these hallucinations often involve costly training or rely heavily on external models, recent approaches utilizing internal model features present a promising alternative. In this paper, we critically assess the limitations of the state-of-the-art training-free technique, the logit lens, in handling generalized visual hallucinations. We introduce ContextualLens, a refined method that leverages contextual token embeddings from middle layers of LMMs. This approach significantly improves hallucination detection and grounding across diverse categories, including actions and OCR, while also excelling in tasks requiring contextual understanding, such as spatial relations and attribute comparison. Our novel grounding technique yields highly precise bounding boxes, facilitating a transition from Zero-Shot Object Segmentation to Grounded Visual Question Answering. Our contributions pave the way for more reliable and interpretable multimodal models.

papers.title: Weakly Supervised Detection of Hallucinations in LLM Activations
papers.research_question: This paper investigates whether pre-trained LLMs encode hallucination patterns in their internal states and proposes a weakly supervised method to detect such patterns without prior knowledge of the anomaly type.
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces a weakly supervised auditing method that uses subset scanning to detect hallucination patterns in LLM activations without requiring labeled anomalous data, achieving performance similar to a supervised classifier.
papers.conclusion: The proposed weakly supervised auditing method can detect hallucinations in LLM activations without needing labeled anomalous data, performing similarly to a supervised baseline, and the identified nodes could be used for targeted fine-tuning.
papers.key_findings:
BERT shows limited internal capacity for encoding hallucinations, while OPT encodes hallucination information effectively.
The weakly supervised scanning method performs comparably to a supervised classifier in detecting hallucinations.
The method can detect anomalies (hallucinations, toxicity, stereotypes) without prior knowledge of the anomaly type.
The method identifies subsets of nodes that are pivotal for encoding anomalous patterns.
The method's performance varies with the amount of anomalous data in the test set.
papers.limitation:
Assumes the reference dataset contains only normal statements, which may not be realistic.
Only has positive predictive ability; cannot confirm the absence of anomalies.
future_direction: Extend the method to reference datasets that contain small amounts of anomalous data or are composed of various data sources.
Use the identified pivotal nodes to guide fine-tuning of sub-networks for bias mitigation.
papers.abstract: We propose an auditing method to identify whether a large language model (LLM) encodes patterns such as hallucinations in its internal states, which may propagate to downstream tasks. We introduce a weakly supervised auditing technique using a subset scanning approach to detect anomalous patterns in LLM activations from pre-trained models. Importantly, our method does not need knowledge of the type of patterns a-priori. Instead, it relies on a reference dataset devoid of anomalies during testing. Further, our approach enables the identification of pivotal nodes responsible for encoding these patterns, which may offer crucial insights for fine-tuning specific sub-networks for bias mitigation. We introduce two new scanning methods to handle LLM activations for anomalous sentences that may deviate from the expected distribution in either direction. Our results confirm prior findings of BERT's limited internal capacity for encoding hallucinations, while OPT appears capable of encoding hallucination information internally. Importantly, our scanning approach, without prior exposure to false statements, performs comparably to a fully supervised out-of-distribution classifier.

papers.title: Exploring Causes and Mitigation of Hallucinations in Large Vision Language Models
papers.research_question: What are the causes of hallucinations in Large Vision Language Models during image captioning, and how can they be mitigated?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces a method to detect and reduce hallucinations in LVLMs by comparing token-level hidden representations from inference passes with and without the image, training a classifier on this difference, and using it to guide a novel decoding strategy.
papers.conclusion: Hallucinations in LVLMs arise as language priors override visual information during generation; the proposed method using hidden state differences effectively reduces these hallucinations.
papers.key_findings:
Hallucinations are more likely to occur in the later parts of generated captions.
LVLMs show inconsistent object recognition between generative and discriminative tasks.
Token probability distributions are highly similar with and without image input, indicating heavy reliance on language priors.
A classifier trained on the difference between hidden states with and without the image can effectively predict token-level hallucinations.
The proposed decoding strategy using this classifier significantly reduces hallucination rates in image captioning.
papers.limitation:
The approach may penalize cases where the description of visual content naturally aligns with statistical patterns learned from training data.
The implementation uses basic vector subtraction without exploring more sophisticated distance metrics.
The classifier is highly model-specific and task-dependent, limiting its applicability to other models or tasks.
The token-level classifier was trained with sentence-level annotations, reducing its ability to make fine-grained judgments about hallucinated content.
future_direction: Developing generalized end-to-end solutions to address hallucinations in LVLMs beyond image captioning.
papers.abstract: Large Vision-Language Models (LVLMs) integrate image encoders with Large Language Models (LLMs) to process multi-modal inputs and perform complex visual tasks. However, they often generate hallucinations by describing non-existent objects or attributes, compromising their reliability. This study analyzes hallucination patterns in image captioning, showing that not all tokens in the generation process are influenced by image input and that image dependency can serve as a useful signal for hallucination detection. To address this, we develop an automated pipeline to identify hallucinated objects and train a token-level classifier using hidden representations from parallel inference passes-with and without image input. Leveraging this classifier, we introduce a decoding strategy that effectively controls hallucination rates in image captioning at inference time.

papers.title: Cross-Layer Attention Probing for Fine-Grained Hallucination Detection
papers.research_question: How can we improve hallucination detection in LLMs by probing activations across the entire residual stream?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Cross-Layer Attention Probing (CLAP), a novel probing technique that uses attention over the residual stream to improve hallucination detection in LLMs, enabling fine-grained detection and integration with mitigation strategies.
papers.conclusion: CLAP is an effective method for detecting and mitigating hallucinations in LLMs by leveraging cross-layer attention over the residual stream, outperforming existing approaches and generalizing well out-of-distribution.
papers.key_findings:
CLAP improves hallucination detection over uncertainty baselines and single-layer probes on multiple LLMs and tasks.
CLAP enables fine-grained detection of hallucinations among sampled responses to the same prompt.
Combining CLAP with mitigation strategies like DoLa reduces hallucination rates while minimizing negative impacts on non-hallucinated responses.
CLAP generalizes better out-of-distribution compared to layer-specific probes and semantic entropy probes.
Ablation studies show that cross-layer attention is crucial for CLAP's performance and generalizability.
papers.limitation:
Focused on small LLMs (2B-8B parameters), leaving scaling to larger LLMs for future work.
The role of each layer within CLAP is not investigated and left for future work.
future_direction: Scaling CLAP to larger LLMs
Investigating the role of each layer within CLAP
papers.abstract: With the large-scale adoption of Large Language Models (LLMs) in various applications, there is a growing reliability concern due to their tendency to generate inaccurate text, i.e. hallucinations. In this work, we propose Cross-Layer Attention Probing (CLAP), a novel activation probing technique for hallucination detection, which processes the LLM activations across the entire residual stream as a joint sequence. Our empirical evaluations using five LLMs and three tasks show that CLAP improves hallucination detection compared to baselines on both greedy decoded responses as well as responses sampled at higher temperatures, thus enabling fine-grained detection, i.e. the ability to disambiguate hallucinations and non-hallucinations among different sampled responses to a given prompt. This allows us to propose a detect-then-mitigate strategy using CLAP to reduce hallucinations and improve LLM reliability compared to direct mitigation approaches. Finally, we show that CLAP maintains high reliability even when applied out-of-distribution.

papers.title: Interpreting and Editing Vision-Language Representations to Mitigate Hallucinations
papers.research_question: How can we interpret and edit the internal image representations of vision-language models to detect and reduce object hallucinations?
papers.core_contribution: We introduce a method to interpret VLM internal image representations via the logit lens and a linear editing algorithm (PROJECT AWAY) that reduces object hallucinations by up to 25.7% while preserving caption accuracy, and also enables zero-shot segmentation.
papers.conclusion: Interpreting and editing VLM internal representations is a promising approach to mitigate hallucinations and can unlock new capabilities like zero-shot segmentation.
papers.key_findings:
Internal confidence from projecting image representations to the vocabulary is higher for objects present in the image than for hallucinated objects.
The logit lens applied to image embeddings can spatially localize objects within the image.
The PROJECT AWAY algorithm effectively removes hallucinated objects from captions with high removal rates (up to 86% individually).
Mass removal of hallucinations reduces overall hallucination rates by up to 25.7% on COCO2014 without degrading accuracy.
The same interpretation method provides zero-shot segmentation performance comparable to state-of-the-art methods.
papers.limitation: At high weight factors (α), the editing can make captions nonsensical by removing both hallucinated and correctly detected objects.
papers.abstract: We investigate the internal representations of vision-language models (VLMs) to address hallucinations, a persistent challenge despite advances in model size and training. We project VLMs' internal image representations to their language vocabulary and observe more confident output probabilities on real objects than hallucinated objects. We additionally use these output probabilities to spatially localize real objects. Building on this approach, we introduce a knowledge erasure algorithm that removes hallucinations by linearly orthogonalizing image features with respect to hallucinated object features. We show that targeted edits to a model's latent representations can reduce hallucinations by up to 25.7% on the COCO2014 dataset while preserving performance. Our findings demonstrate how a deeper understanding of VLMs' latent representations can enhance reliability and enable novel capabilities, such as zero-shot segmentation.

papers.title: Fact Grounded Attention: Eliminating Hallucination in Large Language Models Through Attention Level Knowledge Integration
papers.research_question: How can hallucination in Large Language Models be eliminated by integrating external knowledge directly into the attention mechanism?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Fact Grounded Attention (FGA), a method that biases transformer attention scores with knowledge from an external database via a grounding matrix, a learned gate, and hard vocabulary constraints to improve factual accuracy.
papers.conclusion: FGA demonstrates that targeted architectural modifications combined with external knowledge sources can substantially improve factual reliability, offering a practical path toward more trustworthy language generation in knowledge-intensive domains.
papers.key_findings:
FGA achieves 87.1% accuracy in zero-shot mode and 99.7% with fine-tuning on a technical specifications dataset, compared to a 6.3% baseline.
The method enables sub-second knowledge updates without model retraining.
Ablation studies show all three components (grounding matrix, gate, constraints) are necessary for optimal performance.
The learned gate effectively discriminates between factual and non-factual contexts, preventing over-grounding.
FGA introduces minimal computational overhead (under 3% latency increase).
papers.limitation:
Requires structured facts; procedural knowledge, implicit reasoning, and subjective information remain challenging.
Current entity recognition is rule-based; neural entity linking could improve coverage and accuracy at increased computational cost.
Struggles with complex reasoning requiring multiple facts (multi-hop reasoning).
Deterministic guarantee applies only when specific conditions are satisfied (gate confidence threshold, correct entity linking, KB coverage, allowed token set).
future_direction: Explore hierarchical and compositional fact representations.
Improve entity linking with neural methods.
Develop compositional grounding mechanisms for multi-hop reasoning.
papers.abstract: "The greatest enemy of knowledge is not ignorance, it is the illusion of knowledge." Large Language Models have conquered natural language but remain prisoners of their own probabilistic nature--confidently hallucinating facts they never truly knew. We present Fact Grounded Attention (FGA), a novel architectural modification that transforms unreliable language models into deterministic truth tellers by injecting verifiable knowledge directly into the attention mechanism. Unlike existing approaches that patch hallucinations after generation or prepend retrieved text, FGA intervenes at the mathematical heart of the transformer--the pre-softmax attention scores--creating a model that cannot hallucinate when facts exist in its knowledge base. Our experiments across 1,107 technical queries spanning smartphones, laptops, and electric vehicles demonstrate a transformation from 6.3% accuracy in vanilla Llama 3.2 to 99.7% accuracy with FGA. More critically, knowledge updates occur in under one second without retraining, compared to hours for parameter editing approaches. FGA doesn't just reduce hallucination--it eliminates it entirely for verifiable facts, marking a fundamental shift from probabilistic approximation to deterministic precision in neural language generation.

papers.title: The Hidden Life of Tokens: Reducing Hallucination of Large Vision-Language Models via Visual Information Steering
papers.research_question: How does hallucination emerge and propagate internally during generation in Large Vision-Language Models (LVLMs), and how can it be reduced via inference-time intervention?
papers.core_contribution: This paper introduces VISTA, a training-free inference-time intervention framework that reduces hallucination in LVLMs by reinforcing visual information in the activation space (via Visual Steering Vector) and leveraging early-layer semantic information (via Self-Logits Augmentation).
papers.conclusion: VISTA effectively reduces hallucination in LVLMs while preserving generation quality, establishing visual information steering as a promising direction for enhancing the reliability of multimodal AI systems.
papers.key_findings:
Gradual visual information loss: visually grounded tokens become less favored as generation progresses.
Early excitation: semantically meaningful tokens achieve peak activation in layers earlier than the final layer.
Hidden genuine information: visually grounded tokens not decoded still retain relatively high rankings during inference.
VISTA reduces hallucination by about 40% on average in open-ended generation tasks.
VISTA outperforms existing methods across four benchmarks, four architectures, and three decoding strategies.
papers.limitation:
Optimal hyperparameter settings may vary across different architectures.
The effectiveness of VSV relies on the quality of visual cues extracted by the LVLM's vision encoder.
The current implementation focuses on single-round tasks and may require adaptation for interactive scenarios like visual dialogue.
papers.abstract: Large Vision-Language Models (LVLMs) can reason effectively over both textual and visual inputs, but they tend to hallucinate syntactically coherent yet visually ungrounded contents. In this paper, we investigate the internal dynamics of hallucination by examining the tokens logits ranking throughout the generation process, revealing three key patterns in how LVLMs process information: (1) gradual visual information loss - visually grounded tokens gradually become less favored throughout generation, and (2) early excitation - semantically meaningful tokens achieve peak activation in the layers earlier than the final layer. (3) hidden genuine information - visually grounded tokens though not being eventually decoded still retain relatively high rankings at inference. Based on these insights, we propose VISTA (Visual Information Steering with Token-logit Augmentation), a training-free inference-time intervention framework that reduces hallucination while promoting genuine information. VISTA works by combining two complementary approaches: reinforcing visual information in activation space and leveraging early layer activations to promote semantically meaningful decoding. Compared to existing methods, VISTA requires no external supervision and is applicable to various decoding strategies. Extensive experiments show that VISTA on average reduces hallucination by about 40% on evaluated open-ended generation task, and it consistently outperforms existing methods on four benchmarks across four architectures under three decoding strategies. Code is available at https://github.com/LzVv123456/VISTA.

papers.title: Mitigating Hallucinations in Vision-Language Models through Image-Guided Head Suppression
papers.research_question: Can hallucination in LVLMs be linked to specific model components (attention heads) and can suppressing such heads reduce hallucinations?
papers.core_contribution: The paper identifies that hallucinations in LVLMs can be attributed to image-inattentive attention heads and proposes SPIN, a training-free head suppression strategy that reduces hallucinations without significant computational overhead.
papers.conclusion: SPIN effectively mitigates hallucinations in LVLMs by suppressing image-inattentive attention heads, offering a run-time efficient solution that can be seamlessly integrated during inference.
papers.key_findings:
SPIN reduces hallucination scores (CHAIR) by up to 2.7x while maintaining F1.
SPIN improves throughput by 1.8x compared to existing alternatives.
Hallucination-prone heads are often in earlier layers.
SPIN is effective with greedy and beam-search decoding but less so with nucleus sampling.
SPIN does not require retraining and introduces no additional latency during inference.
papers.limitation:
The method requires access to model weights, limiting applicability to open-source models.
Effectiveness is reduced with sampling-based decoding strategies (e.g., nucleus sampling).
papers.abstract: Despite their remarkable progress in multimodal understanding tasks, large vision language models (LVLMs) often suffer from "hallucinations", generating texts misaligned with the visual context. Existing methods aimed at reducing hallucinations through inference time intervention incur a significant increase in latency. To mitigate this, we present SPIN, a task-agnostic attention-guided head suppression strategy that can be seamlessly integrated during inference, without incurring any significant compute or latency overhead. We investigate whether hallucination in LVLMs can be linked to specific model components. Our analysis suggests that hallucinations can be attributed to a dynamic subset of attention heads in each layer. Leveraging this insight, for each text query token, we selectively suppress attention heads that exhibit low attention to image tokens, keeping the top-K attention heads intact. Extensive evaluations on visual question answering and image description tasks demonstrate the efficacy of SPIN in reducing hallucination scores up to 2.7x while maintaining F1, and improving throughput by 1.8x compared to existing alternatives. Code is available at https://github.com/YUECHE77/SPIN.

papers.title: Cracking the Code of Hallucination in LVLMs with Vision-aware Head Divergence
papers.research_question: What internal mechanisms drive hallucination in large vision-language models, and how can we mitigate it by analyzing attention heads?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces Vision-aware Head Divergence (VHD), a metric to quantify attention head sensitivity to visual context, and Vision-aware Head Reinforcement (VHR), a training-free method to mitigate hallucinations by reinforcing vision-aware attention heads.
papers.conclusion: The work investigates the connection between hallucination and multi-head attention, proposes VHR to strengthen vision-aware heads, and shows that VHR outperforms existing methods in improving alignment with visual information.
papers.key_findings:
Only a few attention heads show significant sensitivity to image context, while the majority exhibit minimal variation.
Words and sentences associated with hallucinations generally correspond to lower T-VHD scores, supporting the role of language bias in hallucination.
VHR outperforms existing decoding methods on hallucination benchmarks with negligible additional time cost.
VHR improves model accuracy on diverse tasks while preserving detailedness and naturalness.
VHR effectively reduces hallucinations by reinforcing vision-aware attention heads, as demonstrated by experiments on multiple LVLMs.
papers.limitation: The analysis and mitigation strategy focus primarily on the multi-head attention mechanism, ignoring other architectural factors such as the vision encoder and FFN modules.
future_direction: Comprehensive interventions spanning the entire model, beyond attention head manipulation.
Further analysis of layer-specific mechanisms in LVLMs.
papers.abstract: Large vision-language models (LVLMs) have made substantial progress in integrating large language models (LLMs) with visual inputs, enabling advanced multimodal reasoning. Despite their success, a persistent challenge is hallucination-where generated text fails to accurately reflect visual content-undermining both accuracy and reliability. Existing methods focus on alignment training or decoding refinements but primarily address symptoms at the generation stage without probing the underlying causes. In this work, we investigate the internal mechanisms driving hallucination in LVLMs, with an emphasis on the multi-head attention module. Specifically, we introduce Vision-aware Head Divergence (VHD), a metric that quantifies the sensitivity of attention head outputs to visual context. Based on this, our findings reveal the presence of vision-aware attention heads that are more attuned to visual information; however, the model's overreliance on its prior language patterns is closely related to hallucinations. Building on these insights, we propose Vision-aware Head Reinforcement (VHR), a training-free approach to mitigate hallucination by enhancing the role of vision-aware attention heads. Extensive experiments demonstrate that our method achieves superior performance compared to state-of-the-art approaches in mitigating hallucinations, while maintaining high efficiency with negligible additional time overhead.

papers.title: Mind Scramble: Unveiling Large Language Model Psychology Via Typoglycemia
papers.research_question: Does LLM possess human-like cognitive processes and mechanisms in reading and comprehending? The paper uses Typoglycemia to explore this.
papers.core_contribution: This paper introduces LLM Psychology, a framework that uses Typoglycemia experiments to study cognitive behaviors of LLMs. It finds that LLMs exhibit human-like behaviors but are fundamentally data-driven, and each LLM has a unique cognitive pattern.
papers.conclusion: The study advances research on aligning LLMs with human cognition and provides evidence that LLMs' abilities are data-driven, offering a case for LLM Psychology.
papers.key_findings:
LLMs demonstrate human-like behaviors on a macro scale, such as slightly lower task accuracy with consuming more tokens and time.
Different LLMs show varying degrees of robustness to scrambled input, making it a democratized benchmark for model evaluation.
The impact of different task types varies, with complex logical tasks (e.g., math) in scrambled format being more challenging.
LLMs' emergent human-like abilities are fundamentally statistical and data-driven, rather than genuinely resembling human cognition.
Each LLM exhibits its unique and consistent 'cognitive pattern' across various tasks, unveiling a general mechanism in its psychology process.
papers.abstract: Research into the external behaviors and internal mechanisms of large language models (LLMs) has shown promise in addressing complex tasks in the physical world. Studies suggest that powerful LLMs, like GPT-4, are beginning to exhibit human-like cognitive abilities, including planning, reasoning, and reflection. In this paper, we introduce a research line and methodology called LLM Psychology, leveraging human psychology experiments to investigate the cognitive behaviors and mechanisms of LLMs. We migrate the Typoglycemia phenomenon from psychology to explore the "mind" of LLMs. Unlike human brains, which rely on context and word patterns to comprehend scrambled text, LLMs use distinct encoding and decoding processes. Through Typoglycemia experiments at the character, word, and sentence levels, we observe: (I) LLMs demonstrate human-like behaviors on a macro scale, such as lower task accuracy and higher token/time consumption; (II) LLMs exhibit varying robustness to scrambled input, making Typoglycemia a benchmark for model evaluation without new datasets; (III) Different task types have varying impacts, with complex logical tasks (e.g., math) being more challenging in scrambled form; (IV) Each LLM has a unique and consistent "cognitive pattern" across tasks, revealing general mechanisms in its psychology process. We provide an in-depth analysis of hidden layers to explain these phenomena, paving the way for future research in LLM Psychology and deeper interpretability.

papers.title: VIB-Probe: Detecting and Mitigating Hallucinations in Vision-Language Models via Variational Information Bottleneck
papers.research_question: How can we detect and mitigate hallucinations in Vision-Language Models by probing internal attention mechanisms?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces VIB-Probe, a framework for hallucination detection and mitigation in VLMs that uses a Variational Information Bottleneck to probe attention head outputs and gradient attribution to identify and suppress hallucination-sensitive heads at inference time.
papers.conclusion: VIB-Probe effectively detects and mitigates hallucinations in VLMs by leveraging internal attention dynamics and the Information Bottleneck principle.
papers.key_findings:
VIB-Probe outperforms existing baselines in hallucination detection across multiple benchmarks and VLMs.
The method shows strong transferability and robustness to image perturbations.
Inference-time mitigation by suppressing top hallucination-sensitive attention heads reduces object hallucinations.
papers.limitation:
Focuses on transformer-based VLMs with standard attention mechanisms, so applicability to other architectures is not explored.
Requires white-box access to the model's internal representations and attention outputs.
papers.abstract: Vision-Language Models (VLMs) have demonstrated remarkable progress in multimodal tasks, but remain susceptible to hallucinations, where generated text deviates from the underlying visual content. Existing hallucination detection methods primarily rely on output logits or external verification tools, often overlooking their internal mechanisms. In this work, we investigate the outputs of internal attention heads, postulating that specific heads carry the primary signals for truthful generation.However, directly probing these high-dimensional states is challenging due to the entanglement of visual-linguistic syntax and noise. To address this, we propose VIB-Probe, a novel hallucination detection and mitigation framework leveraging the Variational Information Bottleneck (VIB) theory. Our method extracts discriminative patterns across layers and heads while filtering out semantic nuisances through the information bottleneck principle. Furthermore, by leveraging the gradients of our VIB probe, we identify attention heads with strong causal influence on hallucinations and introduce an inference-time intervention strategy for hallucination mitigation. Extensive experiments across diverse benchmarks demonstrate that VIB-Probe significantly outperforms existing baselines in both settings. Our code will be made publicly available.

papers.title: Pierce the Mists, Greet the Sky: Decipher Knowledge Overshadowing via Knowledge Circuit Analysis
papers.research_question: What are the origins and internal mechanisms of knowledge overshadowing in large language models during training?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces PHANTOMCIRCUIT, a framework that uses knowledge circuit analysis to dissect the internal mechanisms and training dynamics of knowledge overshadowing in LLMs.
papers.conclusion: PHANTOMCIRCUIT effectively analyzes and detects knowledge overshadowing, offering insights into its mechanisms and a pathway for recovery via circuit optimization.
papers.key_findings:
Higher knowledge popularity (P) and model size (M) cause earlier onset, shorter duration, and quicker recovery from knowledge overshadowing.
Larger dataset size (D) leads to earlier onset but slower recovery from overshadowing.
Knowledge overshadowing dynamics are driven by the co-evolution of subordinate knowledge loss proportion (LP) and relative overshadowing rate (RO).
Attention heads in knowledge circuits that focus on {Xdom, Xsub} are crucial for mitigating overshadowing.
Optimizing the number of edges in knowledge circuits can recover from overshadowing by enhancing attention on key differences.
papers.limitation:
Experiments primarily rely on synthetic data for controlled analysis, limiting generalization to real-world data.
Applicability to practical tasks like multi-hop reasoning and code generation is not yet validated.
Dynamic analysis of knowledge circuits throughout training is computationally intensive, hindering scalability.
future_direction: Validate the conclusions on more complex, noisy real-world data and other model architectures.
Explore applicability to practical tasks like multi-hop reasoning and code generation.
Develop more computationally efficient circuit analysis techniques, such as Information Flow Routes (IFR).
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs), despite their remarkable capabilities, are hampered by hallucinations. A particularly challenging variant, knowledge overshadowing, occurs when one piece of activated knowledge inadvertently masks another relevant piece, leading to erroneous outputs even with high-quality training data. Current understanding of overshadowing is largely confined to inference-time observations, lacking deep insights into its origins and internal mechanisms during model training. Therefore, we introduce PhantomCircuit, a novel framework designed to comprehensively analyze and detect knowledge overshadowing. By innovatively employing knowledge circuit analysis, PhantomCircuit dissects the function of key components in the circuit and how the attention pattern dynamics contribute to the overshadowing phenomenon and its evolution throughout the training process. Extensive experiments demonstrate PhantomCircuit's effectiveness in identifying such instances, offering novel insights into this elusive hallucination and providing the research community with a new methodological lens for its potential mitigation.

papers.title: Causal Tracing of Object Representations in Large Vision Language Models: Mechanistic Interpretability and Hallucination Mitigation
papers.research_question: How do large vision-language models process and represent visual object information, and how can we use this understanding to mitigate object hallucination?
papers.core_contribution: We introduce the Fine-grained Cross-modal Causal Tracing (FCCT) framework to analyze how LVLMs process visual object information, and based on the findings, we propose Intermediate Representation Injection (IRI), a training-free inference-time technique that mitigates object hallucination.
papers.conclusion: The FCCT framework provides comprehensive insights into LVLM internal mechanisms, and the IRI technique effectively mitigates object hallucinations in a training-free, model-agnostic manner.
papers.key_findings:
MHSA of the last token in middle layers plays a critical role in aggregating cross-modal information from visual and textual tokens.
FFNs exhibit a three-stage hierarchical progression for the storage and transfer of visual object representations.
Hidden states show a semantic shift from visual-centric in shallow layers to cross-modal and task-related in deep layers.
The proposed IRI method achieves state-of-the-art hallucination mitigation performance across multiple benchmarks and LVLMs.
IRI preserves inference speed and other foundational model capabilities while mitigating hallucinations.
papers.abstract: Despite the remarkable advancements of Large Vision-Language Models (LVLMs), the mechanistic interpretability remains underexplored. Existing analyses are insufficiently comprehensive and lack examination covering visual and textual tokens, model components, and the full range of layers. This limitation restricts actionable insights to improve the faithfulness of model output and the development of downstream tasks, such as hallucination mitigation. To address this limitation, we introduce Fine-grained Cross-modal Causal Tracing (FCCT) framework, which systematically quantifies the causal effects on visual object perception. FCCT conducts fine-grained analysis covering the full range of visual and textual tokens, three core model components including multi-head self-attention (MHSA), feed-forward networks (FFNs), and hidden states, across all decoder layers. Our analysis is the first to demonstrate that MHSAs of the last token in middle layers play a critical role in aggregating cross-modal information, while FFNs exhibit a three-stage hierarchical progression for the storage and transfer of visual object representations. Building on these insights, we propose Intermediate Representation Injection (IRI), a training-free inference-time technique that reinforces visual object information flow by precisely intervening on cross-modal representations at specific components and layers, thereby enhancing perception and mitigating hallucination. Consistent improvements across five widely used benchmarks and LVLMs demonstrate IRI achieves state-of-the-art performance, while preserving inference speed and other foundational performance.

papers.title: Extracting Visual Facts from Intermediate Layers for Mitigating Hallucinations in Multimodal Large Language Models
papers.research_question: How does prior knowledge in Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) suppress visual factual knowledge at the intermediate layer stage, and how can this be leveraged to mitigate object hallucinations?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes EV A, a training-free decoding method that dynamically selects intermediate layers with rich visual factual knowledge, contrasts their output distributions from multimodal and text-only inputs to extract this knowledge, and integrates it into the final layer to correct hallucinatory outputs.
papers.conclusion: EV A, a train-free decoding method that revises final outputs by extracting visual factual knowledge from intermediate layers, significantly reduces the incidence of hallucinations in MLLMs, highlighting its effectiveness.
papers.key_findings:
Visual factual knowledge and the Jensen-Shannon divergence between intermediate-layer original/prior probability distributions show similar evolutionary trends.
The intermediate layer with the maximum JS divergence contains richer visual factual knowledge.
EV A significantly reduces hallucination rates on benchmarks (POPE, MME, CHAIR) compared to baseline methods like DoLa, VCD, OPERA, and DeCo.
EV A is model-agnostic and seamlessly integrates with various classic decoding strategies (greedy search, nucleus sampling, beam search).
EV A's mechanism of subtracting LLM priors can lead to a decline in the model's original recognition capabilities on some tasks.
papers.limitation: Due to GPU cost constraints, experiments are exclusively conducted on a limited set of MLLMs, without exploring additional models or those with larger parameter scales.
papers.abstract: Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) have made significant strides by combining visual recognition and language understanding to generate content that is both coherent and contextually accurate. However, MLLMs continue to struggle with object hallucinations, where models produce seemingly plausible but factually incorrect outputs, including objects that do not exist in the image. Recent work has revealed that the prior knowledge in MLLMs significantly suppresses visual information in deep layers, causing hallucinatory outputs. However, how these priors suppress visual information at the intermediate layer stage in MLLMs remains unclear. We observe that visual factual knowledge and the differences between intermediate-layer prior/original probability distributions show similar evolutionary trends in intermediate layers. Motivated by this, we introduce Decoding by Extracting Visual Facts (EVA), a simple, training-free method that dynamically selects intermediate layers with the most significant visual factual information. By contrasting the output distributions of the selected layer derived from the original input and pure-text input, EVA extracts visual factual knowledge and proportionally incorporates it into the final layer to correct the output logits. Importantly, EVA is model-agnostic, seamlessly integrates with various classic decoding strategies, and is applicable across different MLLMs. We validate EVA on widely-used benchmarks, and the results show that it significantly reduces hallucination rates compared to baseline methods, underscoring its effectiveness in mitigating hallucinations.

papers.title: On the Universal Truthfulness Hyperplane Inside LLMs
papers.research_question: Does a universal truthfulness hyperplane exist within LLMs that can distinguish factually correct and incorrect outputs?
papers.core_contribution: Increasing the diversity of training datasets significantly enhances the generalization of truthfulness probes, supporting the hypothesis that a universal truthfulness hyperplane exists within LLMs.
papers.conclusion: The findings support the existence of a universal truthfulness hyperplane in LLMs, offering directions for future research on hallucination mitigation.
papers.key_findings:
Probes trained on diverse datasets achieve ~70% cross-task accuracy, outperforming baselines like Self-Eval and Probability.
Attention head outputs are more effective for probing truthfulness than layer residual activations.
Increasing dataset diversity improves generalization more than increasing sample size.
The universal truthfulness hyperplane is more pronounced in advanced models like Mistral-7b and LLaMA2-13b-chat.
Probes trained on single datasets like TruthfulQA fail to generalize out-of-distribution, indicating overfitting.
papers.abstract: While large language models (LLMs) have demonstrated remarkable abilities across various fields, hallucination remains a significant challenge. Recent studies have explored hallucinations through the lens of internal representations, proposing mechanisms to decipher LLMs' adherence to facts. However, these approaches often fail to generalize to out-of-distribution data, leading to concerns about whether internal representation patterns reflect fundamental factual awareness, or only overfit spurious correlations on the specific datasets. In this work, we investigate whether a universal truthfulness hyperplane that distinguishes the model's factually correct and incorrect outputs exists within the model. To this end, we scale up the number of training datasets and conduct an extensive evaluation -- we train the truthfulness hyperplane on a diverse collection of over 40 datasets and examine its cross-task, cross-domain, and in-domain generalization. Our results indicate that increasing the diversity of the training datasets significantly enhances the performance in all scenarios, while the volume of data samples plays a less critical role. This finding supports the optimistic hypothesis that a universal truthfulness hyperplane may indeed exist within the model, offering promising directions for future research.

papers.title: Latent Debate: A Surrogate Framework for Interpreting LLM Thinking
papers.research_question: Can we use latent debate to model the LLM thinking process? Can latent debate identify and interpret hallucinations?
papers.core_contribution: We introduce latent debate, a model-agnostic framework that uses internal arguments to interpret a model's thinking process, instantiate it symbolically as a faithful surrogate for LLM true/false tasks, and demonstrate its utility for hallucination detection.
papers.conclusion: Latent debate is a potential framework for understanding internal mechanisms of LLMs, especially for scenarios where internal (dis)agreements appear during inference.
papers.key_findings:
The latent debate framework achieves high consistency (up to 97%) with original LLM predictions, acting as a faithful structured surrogate model.
Features extracted from latent debate enable competitive hallucination detection performance (e.g., 0.82 average AUROC).
SHAP analysis reveals that a high degree of latent debate, particularly in middle layers, is the strongest predictor of hallucination.
The framework is transparent, training-free, and provides interpretable visualizations of internal supporting and attacking arguments.
future_direction: Improving the target model's capabilities, such as factuality, is left to future work.
papers.abstract: Understanding the internal thinking process of Large Language Models (LLMs) and the cause of hallucinations remains a key challenge. To this end, we introduce latent debate, a novel framework for interpreting model predictions through the lens of implicit internal arguments. Unlike the current work of self-consistency and multi-agent debate, which relies on explicit debates among multiple answers or multiple models, latent debate captures the hidden supporting and attacking signals that arise within a single model during a single inference. We first present a model- and task-agnostic conceptual framework, and then instantiate it symbolically to approximate the thinking process of LLMs on True/False prediction tasks. Empirical studies demonstrate that latent debate is a faithful structured surrogate model that has highly consistent predictions with the original LLM. Beyond interpretability, we demonstrate that latent debate provides a strong baseline for hallucination detection. Further analysis reveals strong correlations between hallucinations and debate patterns, such as a high degree of latent debates in the middle layers is linked to a higher risk of hallucinations. These findings position latent debate as a potential framework for understanding internal mechanisms of LLMs, especially for scenarios where internal (dis)agreements appear during the inference steps.

papers.title: Generalization or Hallucination? Understanding Out-of-Context Reasoning in Transformers
papers.research_question: Does generalization and hallucination on newly-injected factual knowledge arise from the same underlying mechanism?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that generalization and hallucination in LLMs arise from the same mechanism of out-of-context reasoning (OCR), and provides a theoretical analysis of OCR in one-layer transformers, linking it to the implicit bias of gradient descent.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that OCR is a double-edged sword that enables generalization but also leads to hallucination, and their theoretical analysis provides insights into when and why this happens.
papers.key_findings:
OCR drives both generalization and hallucination in LLMs, depending on whether the associated concepts are causally related.
A one-layer single-head attention-only transformer with factorized output and value matrices can learn OCR, while a non-factorized model cannot.
The implicit bias of gradient descent favors solutions that minimize the nuclear norm of the combined output-value matrix, which enables OCR.
The OCR capability depends on the ratio of entities whose fact and implication are both observed during training.
LLMs can learn associations (both causal and spurious) from very few examples, leading to efficient generalization but also vulnerability to hallucination.
papers.limitation: Theoretical results only focus on one-layer transformers.
future_direction: Extend theoretical analysis to multi-layer transformers.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) can acquire new knowledge through fine-tuning, but this process exhibits a puzzling duality: models can generalize remarkably from new facts, yet are also prone to hallucinating incorrect information. However, the reasons for this phenomenon remain poorly understood. In this work, we argue that both behaviors stem from a single mechanism known as out-of-context reasoning (OCR): the ability to deduce implications by associating concepts, even those without a causal link. Our experiments across five prominent LLMs confirm that OCR indeed drives both generalization and hallucination, depending on whether the associated concepts are causally related. To build a rigorous theoretical understanding of this phenomenon, we then formalize OCR as a synthetic factual recall task. We empirically show that a one-layer single-head attention-only transformer with factorized output and value matrices can learn to solve this task, while a model with combined weights cannot, highlighting the crucial role of matrix factorization. Our theoretical analysis shows that the OCR capability can be attributed to the implicit bias of gradient descent, which favors solutions that minimize the nuclear norm of the combined output-value matrix. This mathematical structure explains why the model learns to associate facts and implications with high sample efficiency, regardless of whether the correlation is causal or merely spurious. Ultimately, our work provides a theoretical foundation for understanding the OCR phenomenon, offering a new lens for analyzing and mitigating undesirable behaviors from knowledge injection.

papers.title: On the Effect of Uncertainty on Layer-wise Inference Dynamics
papers.research_question: How does uncertainty affect the inference dynamics of models, and does model competence affect the ability to adapt inference dynamics to uncertainty?
papers.core_contribution: The paper demonstrates that uncertainty does not significantly affect the inference dynamics of LLMs, as probability trajectories for correct and incorrect predictions are aligned. It also provides preliminary evidence that more competent models may exhibit adaptive inference dynamics.
papers.conclusion: LLMs exhibit similar token probability dynamics and tend to commit to final decisions at specific layers largely independent of output uncertainty, but show potential for greater adaptability in inference dynamics as model competence increases.
papers.key_findings:
Probability trajectories for correct and incorrect predictions are strongly aligned across layers, with abrupt increases in confidence at similar layers.
Prediction depth distributions are similar for correct and incorrect answers, indicating the model commits to its output at similar layers regardless of uncertainty.
Weak but consistent positive correlations exist between answer incorrectness and prediction depth across models and datasets.
Positive correlation between task proficiency (measured by Cohen's Kappa) and prediction depth difference suggests adaptive inference dynamics may emerge with greater model competence.
The findings challenge the feasibility of using simplistic methods for uncertainty detection at inference and suggest more nuanced interpretability approaches are needed.
papers.limitation:
The study is exploratory and requires further validation on more models, especially more competent ones.
More rigorous tests are needed, including analyses with varying levels of uncertainty and accounting for hallucination on known knowledge.
future_direction: Further testing on more models to validate the results, especially on more competent models.
More rigorous tests that include analyses using varying levels of uncertainty and accounts for hallucination on known knowledge.
Similar experiments for aleatoric uncertainty for a more thorough investigation.
papers.abstract: Understanding how large language models (LLMs) internally represent and process their predictions is central to detecting uncertainty and preventing hallucinations. While several studies have shown that models encode uncertainty in their hidden states, it is underexplored how this affects the way they process such hidden states. In this work, we demonstrate that the dynamics of output token probabilities across layers for certain and uncertain outputs are largely aligned, revealing that uncertainty does not seem to affect inference dynamics. Specifically, we use the Tuned Lens, a variant of the Logit Lens, to analyze the layer-wise probability trajectories of final prediction tokens across 11 datasets and 5 models. Using incorrect predictions as those with higher epistemic uncertainty, our results show aligned trajectories for certain and uncertain predictions that both observe abrupt increases in confidence at similar layers. We balance this finding by showing evidence that more competent models may learn to process uncertainty differently. Our findings challenge the feasibility of leveraging simplistic methods for detecting uncertainty at inference. More broadly, our work demonstrates how interpretability methods may be used to investigate the way uncertainty affects inference.

papers.title: AFTER: Mitigating the Object Hallucination of LVLM via Adaptive Factual-Guided Activation Editing
papers.research_question: How can object hallucination in Large Vision-Language Models (LVLMs) be mitigated using adaptive factual-guided activation editing?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces AFTER, an activation editing approach that uses factual textual semantics to adaptively steer LVLM activations towards factual semantics, reducing object hallucination with minimal cost.
papers.conclusion: AFTER effectively mitigates object hallucination in LVLMs via adaptive factual-guided activation editing, demonstrating superior performance, generalizability, and preservation of general visual capabilities.
papers.key_findings:
AFTER significantly reduces object hallucination, achieving up to a 16.3% reduction on the AMBER benchmark.
It outperforms state-of-the-art activation editing methods like VTI and ICT on POPE, MME, and AMBER benchmarks.
AFTER enhances general visual capabilities and maintains fast inference speed (29.7 tokens per second).
The method generalizes well to out-of-distribution images and questions, as shown in COCO→GQA and Dis→Gen experiments.
Hyperparameter analysis reveals optimal performance with specific editing strength and number of heads, indicating a trade-off between truthfulness and helpfulness.
papers.limitation:
Dependence on accessible activations from open-source LLMs, which restricts its applicability to closed-source LLMs.
For tasks requiring substantial domain expertise, such as medical report analysis, AFTER necessitates supplementary domain-specific data to enhance LVLM's specialized visual perception.
future_direction: Extend AFTER to encompass a wider range of specialized domains.
papers.abstract: Large Vision-Language Models (LVLMs) have achieved substantial progress in cross-modal tasks. However, due to language bias, LVLMs are susceptible to object hallucination, which can be primarily divided into category, attribute, and relation hallucination, significantly impeding the trustworthy AI applications. Editing the internal activations of LVLMs has shown promising effectiveness in mitigating hallucinations with minimal cost. However, previous editing approaches neglect the effective guidance offered by factual textual semantics, thereby struggling to explicitly mitigate language bias. To address these issues, we propose Adaptive Factual-guided Visual-Textual Editing for hallucination mitigation (AFTER), which comprises Factual-Augmented Activation Steering (FAS) and Query-Adaptive Offset Optimization (QAO), to adaptively guides the original biased activations towards factual semantics. Specifically, FAS is proposed to provide factual and general guidance for activation editing, thereby explicitly modeling the precise visual-textual associations. Subsequently, QAO introduces a query-aware offset estimator to establish query-specific editing from the general steering vector, enhancing the diversity and granularity of editing. Extensive experiments on standard hallucination benchmarks across three widely adopted LVLMs validate the efficacy of the proposed AFTER, notably achieving up to a 16.3% reduction of hallucination over baseline on the AMBER benchmark. Our code and data will be released for reproducibility.

papers.title: Harnessing Reasoning Trajectories for Hallucination Detection via Answer-agreement Representation Shaping
papers.abstract: Large reasoning models (LRMs) often generate long, seemingly coherent reasoning traces yet still produce incorrect answers, making hallucination detection challenging. Although trajectories contain useful signals, directly using trace text or vanilla hidden states for detection is brittle: traces vary in form and detectors can overfit to superficial patterns rather than answer validity.
