papers.conclusion: DoLa is an effective decoding strategy that improves factuality in LLMs across various tasks and model sizes, with minimal computational overhead.
papers.key_findings:
DoLa improves truthfulness on TruthfulQA by 12-17% absolute points across LLaMA models.
DoLa improves factuality on FACTOR, a long-paragraph factuality benchmark.
DoLa improves performance on chain-of-thought reasoning tasks (StrategyQA and GSM8K).
DoLa generates more factual and informative responses in open-ended chatbot evaluation (Vicuna QA) as rated by GPT-4.
DoLa introduces only a small latency overhead (1.01-1.08x) during decoding.
papers.limitation:
DoLa may not work well for small language models (e.g., GPT2) due to limited capacity and lack of distinct layer representations.
DoLa sometimes generates detailed factual information that may be less relevant to the question, indicating a trade-off between factuality and instruction following.
future_direction: Applying DoLa to other model families and tasks.
Exploring integration with instruction tuning.
Improving the ability to follow instructions while maintaining factuality.
papers.abstract: Despite their impressive capabilities, large language models (LLMs) are prone to hallucinations, i.e., generating content that deviates from facts seen during pretraining. We propose a simple decoding strategy for reducing hallucinations with pretrained LLMs that does not require conditioning on retrieved external knowledge nor additional fine-tuning. Our approach obtains the next-token distribution by contrasting the differences in logits obtained from projecting the later layers versus earlier layers to the vocabulary space, exploiting the fact that factual knowledge in an LLMs has generally been shown to be localized to particular transformer layers. We find that this Decoding by Contrasting Layers (DoLa) approach is able to better surface factual knowledge and reduce the generation of incorrect facts. DoLa consistently improves the truthfulness across multiple choices tasks and open-ended generation tasks, for example improving the performance of LLaMA family models on TruthfulQA by 12-17% absolute points, demonstrating its potential in making LLMs reliably generate truthful facts.

papers.title: Mitigating Hallucination in Multimodal Reasoning via Functional Attention Control
papers.research_question: Under off-the-shelf architectures, how can we effectively identify and regulate the use of visual and textual information at different stages to mitigate hallucinations in multimodal large reasoning models?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes a lightweight, training-free plugin that identifies perception- and reasoning-oriented attention heads and adaptively rebalances their layerwise contributions to reduce multimodal hallucinations by countering perceptual bias and reasoning drift.
papers.conclusion: The study provides an interpretable perspective on regulating cross-layer functional dynamics to enhance the reliability of multimodal reasoning, demonstrating that lightweight, targeted interventions on attention heads can significantly mitigate hallucinations.
papers.key_findings:
The method decomposes hallucinations into two primary failure causes: Perceptual Bias in shallow layers and Reasoning Drift in deeper layers.
The proposed plugin improves reasoning consistency and visual faithfulness without retraining or architectural modification.
Evaluations across three MLRMs and five benchmarks show an average 4.2-percentage-point gain, with less than 1% additional computation and only 9% baseline latency.
Ablation studies show that perception-only and reasoning-only rescaling have task-skewed and non-additive effects, highlighting the need for joint optimization.
The method's effectiveness is stable across a broad operating region of hyperparameters, reducing concerns about sensitivity to fine-grained tuning.
papers.limitation: The method's performance may be sensitive to the choice of layer boundaries and visual-attention ratio thresholds, although experiments indicate stability within a broad operating region.
future_direction: Extending the method to other multimodal architectures beyond the transformer-based models studied.
Investigating the applicability of the approach to other types of hallucinations, such as those arising from insufficient knowledge or decoding bias.
papers.abstract: Multimodal large reasoning models (MLRMs) are rapidly advancing vision-language reasoning and are emerging as a foundation for cross-modal intelligence. Hallucination remains a persistent failure mode, manifesting itself as erroneous reasoning chains and misinterpretation of visual content. In this study, we observe that attention heads exhibit a staged division: shallow heads predominantly serve perception, while deeper heads shift toward symbolic reasoning, revealing two major causes of hallucination, namely perceptual bias and reasoning drift. To address these issues, we propose a lightweight and interpretable two-step plugin, Functional Head Identification and Class-conditioned Rescaling, which locates perception- and reasoning-oriented heads and regulates their contributions without retraining. Evaluations on three real-world MLRMs (Kimi-VL, Ocean-R1, R1-Onevision), six benchmarks across three domains, and four baselines show that our plugin achieves an average improvement of 5% and up to 15%, with only <1% additional computation and 9% of baseline latency. Our approach is completely model-agnostic and significantly enhances both the reliability and interpretability of the off-the-shelf MLRMs, thereby enabling their safe deployment in high-stakes applications. Our code is available at https://anonymous.4open.science/r/Functional-Attention-Control.

papers.title: Indications of Belief-Guided Agency and Meta-Cognitive Monitoring in Large Language Models
papers.research_question: Does the behavior of large language models indicate belief-guided agency and meta-cognitive monitoring as defined by the HOT-3 indicator for consciousness?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a framework and the Belief Dominance metric to test the HOT-3 indicator in LLMs, providing empirical evidence for belief-guided agency and meta-cognitive monitoring.
papers.conclusion: The work demonstrates the existence of agency guided by a general belief formation and action selection system regulated by meta-cognitive monitoring in LLMs, contributing to the study of AI consciousness.
papers.key_findings:
External manipulations systematically modulate internal belief formation.
Belief formation causally drives the model's action selection.
Models can monitor and report their own belief states, indicating meta-cognitive monitoring.
papers.limitation:
The mechanistic implementation of belief formation, action selection, and meta-cognition remains unclear.
The framework is restricted to capturing beliefs that can be expressed in words.
The framework currently only tests two competing beliefs.
future_direction: Studying the mechanistic implementation of belief formation and meta-cognitive monitoring.
Extending the framework to capture latent beliefs beyond existing vocabulary.
Testing additional consciousness criteria in more capable models.
papers.abstract: Rapid advancements in large language models (LLMs) have sparked the question whether these models possess some form of consciousness. To tackle this challenge, Butlin et al. (2023) introduced a list of indicators for consciousness in artificial systems based on neuroscientific theories. In this work, we evaluate a key indicator from this list, called HOT-3, which tests for agency guided by a general belief-formation and action selection system that updates beliefs based on meta-cognitive monitoring. We view beliefs as representations in the model's latent space that emerge in response to a given input, and introduce a metric to quantify their dominance during generation. Analyzing the dynamics between competing beliefs across models and tasks reveals three key findings: (1) external manipulations systematically modulate internal belief formation, (2) belief formation causally drives the model's action selection, and (3) models can monitor and report their own belief states. Together, these results provide empirical support for the existence of belief-guided agency and meta-cognitive monitoring in LLMs. More broadly, our work lays methodological groundwork for investigating the emergence of agency, beliefs, and meta-cognition in LLMs.

papers.title: Internal Representations as Indicators of Hallucinations in Agent Tool Selection
papers.research_question: Can internal representations of LLMs be used to detect tool-calling hallucinations in real-time?
papers.core_contribution: Presents a computationally efficient framework for real-time detection of tool-calling hallucinations by leveraging LLMs' internal representations during generation, achieving up to 86.4% accuracy with minimal overhead.
papers.conclusion: Internal representations of LLMs can be effectively used for real-time detection of tool-calling hallucinations, providing a practical solution for deployment in production agent systems with minimal computational overhead.
papers.key_findings:
Internal representations of LLMs contain discriminative information for detecting tool-calling hallucinations.
The method achieves up to 86.4% accuracy in hallucination detection across multiple models.
The approach operates in real-time using only last-layer representations from a single forward pass, with minimal computational overhead.
The method shows higher recall compared to baseline methods like Non Contradiction Probability and semantic similarity for some models.
Simple feature extraction methods (e.g., mean pooling) are effective for hallucination detection, with diminishing returns for more complex aggregation.
papers.limitation:
Reference-agreement labeling inherits problems from dataset calls and standardization rules.
Determining function equivalence beyond string matching remains difficult without additional context.
The three-point feature design is intentionally simple and may be improved.
future_direction: Developing a unified hallucination detector that works effectively across different model families.
Exploring field-aware pooling or lightweight attention over argument spans while keeping single-pass requirements.
Expanding experiments, accuracy analysis, and robustness studies across new tools.
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have shown remarkable capabilities in tool calling and tool usage, but suffer from hallucinations where they choose incorrect tools, provide malformed parameters and exhibit 'tool bypass' behavior by performing simulations and generating outputs instead of invoking specialized tools or external systems. This undermines the reliability of LLM based agents in production systems as it leads to inconsistent results, and bypasses security and audit controls. Such hallucinations in agent tool selection require early detection and error handling. Unlike existing hallucination detection methods that require multiple forward passes or external validation, we present a computationally efficient framework that detects tool-calling hallucinations in real-time by leveraging LLMs' internal representations during the same forward pass used for generation. We evaluate this approach on reasoning tasks across multiple domains, demonstrating strong detection performance (up to 86.4\% accuracy) while maintaining real-time inference capabilities with minimal computational overhead, particularly excelling at detecting parameter-level hallucinations and inappropriate tool selections, critical for reliable agent deployment.

papers.title: DeCoRe: Decoding by Contrasting Retrieval Heads to Mitigate Hallucinations
papers.research_question: Can masking retrieval heads induce hallucinations, and can contrasting the outputs of the base LLM and the masked LLM reduce hallucinations, specifically improving contextual faithfulness, factual recall, and multi-hop reasoning?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes DeCoRe, a training-free decoding strategy that contrasts base and masked LLM outputs to mitigate hallucinations, using conditional entropy to dynamically control the contrast.
papers.conclusion: DeCoRe effectively mitigates hallucinations by contrasting base and masked LLM outputs, improving faithfulness, factuality, and reasoning across multiple tasks and models.
papers.key_findings:
DeCoRe significantly improves contextual faithfulness on summarization (XSum), instruction following (MemoTrap), and open-book QA (NQ-Open, NQ-Swap).
DeCoRe improves factual recall on TriviaQA, PopQA, and TruthfulQA, indicating it mitigates factuality hallucinations.
DeCoRe enhances multi-hop reasoning when combined with Chain-of-Thought prompting, as shown on MuSiQue.
Masking retrieval heads induces hallucinations, validating their role in information retrieval.
Dynamic entropy-controlled contrastive decoding (DeCoRe_entropy) outperforms static versions and baselines in many tasks.
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) often hallucinate, producing unfaithful or factually incorrect outputs by misrepresenting the provided context or incorrectly recalling internal knowledge. Recent studies have identified specific attention heads within the Transformer architecture, known as retrieval heads, responsible for extracting relevant contextual information. We hypothesise that masking these retrieval heads can induce hallucinations and that contrasting the outputs of the base LLM and the masked LLM can reduce hallucinations. To this end, we propose Decoding by Contrasting Retrieval Heads (DeCoRe), a novel training-free decoding strategy that amplifies information found in the context and model parameters. DeCoRe mitigates potentially hallucinated responses by dynamically contrasting the outputs of the base LLM and the masked LLM, using conditional entropy as a guide. Our extensive experiments confirm that DeCoRe significantly improves performance on tasks requiring high contextual faithfulness, such as summarisation (XSum by 18.6%), instruction following (MemoTrap by 10.9%), and open-book question answering (NQ-Open by 2.4% and NQ-Swap by 5.5%).

papers.title: DRIFT: Detecting Representational Inconsistencies for Factual Truthfulness
papers.research_question: Can intermediate layers of LLMs encode confidence signals that are lost in the final output, and can a lightweight probe read these signals to detect hallucinations efficiently and accurately?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes a lightweight hallucination detector that reads uncertainty signals from intermediate hidden states with less than 0.1% computational overhead, enabling parallel detection and an LLM router for selective prediction.
papers.conclusion: Intermediate representations in LLMs encode confidence signals that can be effectively read by a lightweight probe for efficient hallucination detection and selective prediction, enabling zero-latency routing for confident queries.
papers.key_findings:
Intermediate-layer representations outperform final-layer representations for hallucination detection.
The method achieves state-of-the-art AUROC on 10 out of 12 settings across four QA benchmarks and three LLM families.
The detector generalizes well across dataset shifts without retraining.
Detection performance improves with larger model scale.
Using answer token representations yields higher accuracy than question-only representations, but question-only detection already outperforms baselines.
papers.limitation:
Experiments focus on single-turn, closed-book question answering and do not test on multi-turn dialogues, tool use, code generation, or summarization.
Correctness is used as a proxy for hallucination, which may not capture all error types (e.g., systematic errors from training data or logical reasoning errors).
Some model-dataset combinations exhibit severe label imbalance, which may affect results.
future_direction: Applying the uncertainty signal to guide exploration in reinforcement learning for LLMs, such as in Monte Carlo tree search algorithms.
Adapting the method to other scenarios like multi-turn dialogues, which requires collecting corresponding training data and potentially using compression or sliding-window strategies.
papers.abstract: LLMs often produce fluent but incorrect answers, yet detecting such hallucinations typically requires multiple sampling passes or post-hoc verification, adding significant latency and cost. We hypothesize that intermediate layers encode confidence signals that are lost in the final output layer, and propose a lightweight probe to read these signals directly from hidden states. The probe adds less than 0.1\% computational overhead and can run fully in parallel with generation, enabling hallucination detection before the answer is produced. Building on this, we develop an LLM router that answers confident queries immediately while delegating uncertain ones to stronger models. Despite its simplicity, our method achieves SOTA AUROC on 10 out of 12 settings across four QA benchmarks and three LLM families, with gains of up to 13 points over prior methods, and generalizes across dataset shifts without retraining.

papers.title: The Curious Case of Analogies: Investigating Analogical Reasoning in Large Language Models
papers.research_question: How do large language models encode and apply high-level relational concepts for analogical reasoning, and how do they structurally align analogous situations?
papers.core_contribution: The paper investigates the internal mechanisms of analogical reasoning in LLMs, finding that they encode relational information in mid-upper layers but struggle to apply it, and that successful reasoning is associated with strong structural alignment between analogous situations.
papers.conclusion: LLMs show emerging but limited capabilities in analogical reasoning, with parallels to human cognition in encoding relational information and structural alignment, but gaps in application and alignment.
papers.key_findings:
LLMs effectively encode underlying relationships between analogous entities in mid-upper layers, with relational information being a key factor for correct reasoning.
LLMs struggle not only when relational information is missing but also when attempting to apply it to new entities.
Strategically patching hidden representations at critical token positions can facilitate information transfer and improve performance.
Successful analogical reasoning is marked by strong structural alignment between analogous situations, while failures show degraded alignment.
Analogical structure becomes linearly separable in middle layers, and token-level alignment (measured by Mutual Alignment Score) is higher for correct analogies.
future_direction: Future research into understanding and improving the analogical reasoning capabilities of LLMs.
papers.abstract: Analogical reasoning is at the core of human cognition, serving as an important foundation for a variety of intellectual activities. While prior work has shown that LLMs can represent task patterns and surface-level concepts, it remains unclear whether these models can encode high-level relational concepts and apply them to novel situations through structured comparisons. In this work, we explore this fundamental aspect using proportional and story analogies, and identify three key findings. First, LLMs effectively encode the underlying relationships between analogous entities; both attributive and relational information propagate through mid-upper layers in correct cases, whereas reasoning failures reflect missing relational information within these layers. Second, unlike humans, LLMs often struggle not only when relational information is missing, but also when attempting to apply it to new entities. In such cases, strategically patching hidden representations at critical token positions can facilitate information transfer to a certain extent. Lastly, successful analogical reasoning in LLMs is marked by strong structural alignment between analogous situations, whereas failures often reflect degraded or misplaced alignment. Overall, our findings reveal that LLMs exhibit emerging but limited capabilities in encoding and applying high-level relational concepts, highlighting both parallels and gaps with human cognition.

papers.title: Listen to the Layers: Mitigating Hallucinations with Inter-Layer Disagreement
papers.research_question: How can inter-layer disagreement in LLMs be used to mitigate hallucinations and improve factual correctness?
papers.core_contribution: The paper proposes CoCoA, a training-free decoding algorithm that mitigates hallucinations by penalizing outputs with high inter-layer disagreement in the middle layers of LLMs.
papers.conclusion: CoCoA provides an effective and broadly applicable method for enhancing LLM trustworthiness at inference time by using model-intrinsic signals without requiring retraining.
papers.key_findings:
CoCoA significantly improves factual correctness on TruthfulQA, with improvements in T×I score.
It outperforms baselines like DoLa, DeCoRe, and Diver on multiple tasks including question-answering, summarization, math, and code generation.
The self-information gated variant CoCoA-SIG further enhances performance by dynamically modulating the penalty based on token surprise.
CoCoA works without any model retraining, leveraging intrinsic signals from the model's middle layers.
The method is effective across diverse model families and sizes, demonstrating generalizability.
papers.abstract: Pretrained Large Language Models (LLMs) are prone to generating fluent yet factually incorrect text-a phenomenon known as hallucinations, undermining their reliability and utility in downstream tasks. We hypothesize that a generated text span's factuality is correlated with its representational instability across the model's internal layers. Based on this, we propose the CoCoA (Confusion and Consistency Aware) decoder, a novel, training-free decoding algorithm that mitigates hallucinations at inference time by listening to these signals in the middle layers. We propose two metrics to quantify this instability in the middle layers, and use it to penalize outputs that exhibit high internal confusion, thereby steering the model towards more internally consistent and factually grounded outputs. We further propose a self-information gated variant, CoCoA-SIG, that dynamically modulates this penalty to selectively target high-surprise, unstable generations. Extensive experiments on diverse tasks, including question-answering, summarization and code generation demonstrate that CoCoA significantly improves factual correctness across multiple model families (e.g., Llama-3, Qwen-2.5, Mistral). By leveraging model-intrinsic signals, CoCoA offers an effective and broadly applicable method for enhancing the trustworthiness of LLMs at inference time, without requiring any model retraining.

papers.title: SAFE: A Sparse Autoencoder-Based Framework for Robust Query Enrichment and Hallucination Mitigation in LLMs
papers.research_question: Can we harness the creative power of LLMs while mitigating their hallucinations by steering the model to leverage its existing knowledge more effectively using Sparse Autoencoders?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes SAFE, a two-stage framework that first detects hallucinations via entropy-based uncertainty estimation and then mitigates them by enriching the query with SAE-derived features, improving accuracy without additional training.
papers.conclusion: SAFE significantly reduces hallucination rates and improves response accuracy by up to 29.45% in a training-free, plug-and-play manner, offering a practical solution for enhancing LLM reliability.
papers.key_findings:
SAFE improves accuracy on hallucination-prone QA datasets across different models and architectures.
Ablation studies confirm the critical role of entropy-based detection and SAE-driven enrichment in achieving performance gains.
SAFE can make smaller models perform comparably to larger ones in some cases, as shown by the comparison with Gemma2-27b and Llama3-70b.
The framework operates in a training-free manner, offering a lightweight, plug-and-play solution.
papers.limitation:
Reliance on an SAE and the availability of auto-interpretable features constrains its applicability to LLMs that expose such internal representations.
Effectiveness is influenced by the quality of the input queries.
Current implementation is restricted to English-language inputs.
future_direction: Extending the approach to models without SAE characteristics would require modifications or alternative interpretability techniques.
Multilingual and multimodal extensions are promising directions for future research.
papers.abstract: Despite the state-of-the-art performance of Large Language Models (LLMs), these models often suffer from hallucinations, which can undermine their performance in critical applications. In this work, we propose SAFE, a novel method for detecting and mitigating hallucinations by leveraging Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs). While hallucination detection techniques and SAEs have been explored independently, their synergistic application in a comprehensive system, particularly for hallucination-aware query enrichment, has not been fully investigated. To validate the effectiveness of SAFE, we evaluate it on two models with available SAEs across three diverse cross-domain datasets designed to assess hallucination problems. Empirical results demonstrate that SAFE consistently improves query generation accuracy and mitigates hallucinations across all datasets, achieving accuracy improvements of up to 29.45%.

papers.title: A Graph Signal Processing Framework for Hallucination Detection in Large Language Models
papers.research_question: Can spectral analysis of transformer layers, modeled as dynamic graphs induced by attention, be used to detect hallucinations in large language models? Do different types of hallucinations exhibit distinct spectral signatures?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes a spectral analysis framework for hallucination detection in LLMs, showing that factual reasoning exhibits universal spectral patterns (energy mountain, low-frequency convergence) while hallucinations show distinct signatures.
papers.conclusion: The spectral graph processing framework reveals universal convergence patterns in factual reasoning and distinct spectral fingerprints for hallucinations, establishing spectral geometry as both an interpretive lens and a diagnostic tool for monitoring LLMs.
papers.key_findings:
Factual statements exhibit consistent 'energy mountain' behavior with low-frequency convergence across architectures.
Logical hallucinations destabilize spectra with large effect sizes, semantic hallucinations show connectivity drift and entropy rise, and substitution hallucinations exhibit intermediate perturbations.
A simple detector using spectral signatures (SHD) achieves 88.75% accuracy, outperforming perplexity-based baselines (75%).
Spectral geometry captures reasoning patterns and error behaviors, offering a framework for hallucination detection.
papers.limitation: Semantic hallucinations often remain within factual variance for primary metrics (HFER, entropy, SMI), requiring subtler secondary signatures (Fiedler drift) for detection.
future_direction: building adaptive detectors for real-time monitoring
studying larger architectures
exploring connections between spectral geometry and linguistic structure
papers.abstract: Large language models achieve impressive results but distinguishing factual reasoning from hallucinations remains challenging. We propose a spectral analysis framework that models transformer layers as dynamic graphs induced by attention, with token embeddings as signals on these graphs. Through graph signal processing, we define diagnostics including Dirichlet energy, spectral entropy, and high-frequency energy ratios, with theoretical connections to computational stability. Experiments across GPT architectures suggest universal spectral patterns: factual statements exhibit consistent "energy mountain" behavior with low-frequency convergence, while different hallucination types show distinct signatures. Logical contradictions destabilize spectra with large effect sizes ($g>1.0$), semantic errors remain stable but show connectivity drift, and substitution hallucinations display intermediate perturbations. A simple detector using spectral signatures achieves 88.75% accuracy versus 75% for perplexity-based baselines, demonstrating practical utility. These findings indicate that spectral geometry may capture reasoning patterns and error behaviors, potentially offering a framework for hallucination detection in large language models.

papers.title: Mitigating Object Hallucinations in Large Vision-Language Models via Attention Calibration
papers.research_question: How can object hallucination in Large Vision-Language Models (LVLMs) be mitigated by addressing spatial perception bias in attention maps?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Dynamic Attention Calibration (DAC), a lightweight, plug-and-play module that dynamically calibrates vision token attention to mitigate spatial perception bias and reduce object hallucination in LVLMs.
papers.conclusion: Attention calibration, specifically through the proposed Dynamic Attention Calibration (DAC) module, is a promising strategy for mitigating object hallucination in LVLMs by dynamically addressing spatial perception bias.
papers.key_findings:
DAC significantly reduces object hallucination on POPE benchmarks, achieving state-of-the-art performance across Random, Popular, and Adversarial settings.
DAC improves performance on the CHAIR metric for open-ended image captioning, reducing hallucinated objects in generated descriptions.
DAC enhances general perception capabilities on the MME benchmark, particularly in object-level and attribute-level tasks.
DAC maintains or improves performance on the LLaVA-Bench, indicating it does not degrade general vision-language understanding.
The method is effective across multiple LVLM architectures (LLaVA-1.5, mPLUG-Owl2, LLaVA-NeXT), demonstrating generalizability.
papers.limitation: DAC's performance may be limited when validation data is scarce.
future_direction: Explore data-free calibration methods.
Extend attention calibration to further improve LVLMs reliability.
papers.abstract: Large Vision-Language Models (LVLMs) exhibit impressive multimodal reasoning capabilities but remain highly susceptible to object hallucination, where models generate responses that are not factually aligned with the visual content. Recent works attribute this issue to an inherent bias of LVLMs where vision token attention map has a fixed correlation with spatial position, and propose to mitigate this issue by reordering visual tokens. However, we find that different LVLMs exhibit different correlations between attention and spatial position, which makes the existing solution difficult to generalize to other LVLMs. To address this issue, we first introduce a training-free solution, Uniform Attention Calibration (UAC), that estimates the bias from single meaningless input image and applies a calibration matrix to rectify attention imbalances. To further alleviate the bias, we relax the assumption of single meaningless input in UAC and introduce a fine-tuning solution, Dynamic Attention Calibration (DAC), that enforces the consistent outputs wherever the object locates in the image via a plug-and-plays module. Comprehensive experiments across multiple benchmarks demonstrate that UAC and DAC significantly reduce object hallucination while improving general multimodal alignment. Our methods achieve state-of-the-art performance across diverse LVLM architectures on various metrics.

papers.title: Adaptive Residual-Update Steering for Low-Overhead Hallucination Mitigation in Large Vision Language Models
papers.research_question: Can we identify a stable, informative and low-cost signal within the model’s standard computational flow to ground generation without introducing extra forward passes?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces RUDDER, a low-overhead inference-time framework that mitigates object hallucination in LVLMs by extracting a visual evidence vector (CARD) from a single forward pass and adaptively injecting it via a Bayesian-inspired gate, achieving state-of-the-art comparable performance with negligible computational overhead.
papers.conclusion: RUDDER presents a practical and effective solution for enhancing the reliability of LVLMs in real-world settings by mitigating hallucination with negligible computational overhead.
papers.key_findings:
RUDDER significantly reduces object hallucination on CHAIR and POPE benchmarks, achieving performance comparable to state-of-the-art methods like VISTA.
RUDDER introduces negligible computational latency, maintaining ~96% of the vanilla model's throughput, unlike methods requiring extra forward passes.
The adaptive Beta Gate provides token-wise precision, allowing strong corrective signals only when the model's generation deviates from visual evidence.
RUDDER's effectiveness generalizes across diverse LVLM architectures (LLaVA, Idefics2, InstructBLIP) and decoding strategies (greedy, beam search, nucleus sampling).
The method does not harm the model's general multimodal capabilities, as validated by stable or improved scores on the MME benchmark.
papers.limitation: RUDDER’s primary limitation is its sensitivity to hyperparameters, which must be tuned for each model architecture.
future_direction: Future work could focus on automated hyperparameter optimization to improve its robustness and ease of deployment.
papers.abstract: Large Vision-Language Models (LVLMs) often suffer from object hallucination, generating text inconsistent with visual inputs, which can critically undermine their reliability. Existing inference-time interventions to mitigate this issue present a challenging trade-off: while methods that steer internal states or adjust output logits can be effective, they often incur substantial computational overhead, typically requiring extra forward passes. This efficiency bottleneck can limit their practicality for real-world, latency-sensitive deployments. In this work, we aim to address this trade-off with Residual-Update Directed DEcoding Regulation (RUDDER), a low-overhead framework that steers LVLMs towards visually-grounded generation. RUDDER is built on two key innovations: (1) Contextual Activation Residual Direction (CARD) vector, a per-sample visual evidence vector extracted from the residual update of a self-attention layer during a single, standard forward pass. (2) A Bayesian-inspired adaptive gate that performs token-wise injection, applying a corrective signal whose strength is conditioned on the model's deviation from the visual context. Extensive experiments on key hallucination benchmarks, including POPE and CHAIR, indicate that RUDDER achieves performance comparable to state-of-the-art methods while introducing negligible computational latency, validating RUDDER as a pragmatic and effective approach for improving LVLMs' reliability without a significant compromise on efficiency.

papers.title: How Post-Training Reshapes LLMs: A Mechanistic View on Knowledge, Truthfulness, Refusal, and Confidence
papers.research_question: How does post-training affect the internal mechanisms of large language models in terms of knowledge storage, truthfulness, refusal, and confidence?
papers.core_contribution: This paper provides a mechanistic analysis of how post-training affects LLMs internally, revealing which mechanisms are preserved (e.g., knowledge storage locations, truthfulness direction) and which are altered (e.g., refusal direction), with implications for model steering and interpretability.
papers.conclusion: Post-training preserves some internal mechanisms (like knowledge storage and truthfulness direction) and alters others (like refusal direction), providing insights for model steering and future research in interpretability and LLM post-training.
papers.key_findings:
Post-training does not change the factual knowledge storage locations in LLMs.
Post-training adapts knowledge representations from the base model while also developing new ones.
The truthfulness direction is highly similar between base and post-trained models and is effectively transferable for interventions.
The refusal direction differs between base and post-trained models and shows limited forward transferability.
Differences in confidence between base and post-trained models cannot be attributed to entropy neurons.
papers.limitation: Complex, multi-step processes such as reasoning and instruction-following are not well-captured by current mechanistic interpretability tools, limiting the scope of analysis.
future_direction: Design better post-training methods based on mechanistic insights.
Extend analysis to other capabilities like reasoning and instruction-following.
papers.abstract: Post-training is essential for the success of large language models (LLMs), transforming pre-trained base models into more useful and aligned post-trained models. While plenty of works have studied post-training algorithms and evaluated post-training models by their outputs, it remains understudied how post-training reshapes LLMs internally. In this paper, we compare base and post-trained LLMs mechanistically from four perspectives to better understand post-training effects. Our findings across model families and datasets reveal that: (1) Post-training does not change the factual knowledge storage locations, and it adapts knowledge representations from the base model while developing new knowledge representations; (2) Both truthfulness and refusal can be represented by vectors in the hidden representation space. The truthfulness direction is highly similar between the base and post-trained model, and it is effectively transferable for interventions; (3) The refusal direction is different between the base and post-trained models, and it shows limited forward transferability; (4) Differences in confidence between the base and post-trained models cannot be attributed to entropy neurons. Our study provides insights into the fundamental mechanisms preserved and altered during post-training, facilitates downstream tasks like model steering, and could potentially benefit future research in interpretability and LLM post-training. Our code is publicly available at https://github.com/HZD01/post-training-mechanistic-analysis.

papers.title: Factual Self-Awareness in Language Models: Representation, Robustness, and Scaling
papers.research_question: Do language models have an internal compass that dictates the correctness of factual recall at the time of generation? Specifically, are there linear features in the Transformer's residual stream that indicate whether the model will recall a correct attribute?
papers.core_contribution: Language models encode linear features in the residual stream that indicate whether they will correctly recall a factual attribute, and this self-awareness signal is robust to formatting variations and emerges early in training.
papers.conclusion: Language models possess intrinsic self-monitoring capabilities for factual recall, which contributes to their interpretability and reliability.
papers.key_findings:
Linear probes and sparse autoencoders (SAEs) show that factual self-awareness is encoded as linear directions in the residual stream, separable between known and forgotten factual associations.
The self-awareness signal is robust to superficial perturbations like quotation marks, but sensitive to structural changes like rephrasing as questions.
The signal emerges rapidly during training and peaks in intermediate layers.
Larger models (within a family) do not necessarily have more linearly decodable self-awareness representations.
The class balance of known and forgotten samples depends on the sampling parameters (k, l) used to define them.
papers.limitation:
Defining knowledge at the entity level is a limitation: when an LM fabricates factual associations, it may invent attributes for a known entity.
Some input templates introduced spurious correlations due to their phrasing, which had to be excluded.
papers.abstract: Factual incorrectness in generated content is one of the primary concerns in ubiquitous deployment of large language models (LLMs). Prior findings suggest LLMs can (sometimes) detect factual incorrectness in their generated content (i.e., fact-checking post-generation). In this work, we provide evidence supporting the presence of LLMs' internal compass that dictate the correctness of factual recall at the time of generation. We demonstrate that for a given subject entity and a relation, LLMs internally encode linear features in the Transformer's residual stream that dictate whether it will be able to recall the correct attribute (that forms a valid entity-relation-attribute triplet). This self-awareness signal is robust to minor formatting variations. We investigate the effects of context perturbation via different example selection strategies. Scaling experiments across model sizes and training dynamics highlight that self-awareness emerges rapidly during training and peaks in intermediate layers. These findings uncover intrinsic self-monitoring capabilities within LLMs, contributing to their interpretability and reliability.

papers.title: Uncertainty Unveiled: Can Exposure to More In-context Examples Mitigate Uncertainty for Large Language Models?
papers.research_question: How does increasing the number of in-context examples influence the predictive uncertainty of large language models in in-context learning?
papers.core_contribution: Additional in-context examples reduce total uncertainty in LLMs by injecting task-specific knowledge, which primarily diminishes epistemic uncertainty and enhances performance.
papers.conclusion: Additional examples reduce uncertainty by integrating task-specific knowledge, primarily through reducing epistemic uncertainty, and many-shot ICL increases model confidence by reallocating logit mass and enlarging the logit margin.
papers.key_findings:
Additional in-context examples reduce total uncertainty (TU) in both simple and complex tasks.
The reduction in TU is primarily driven by a decrease in epistemic uncertainty (EU).
For complex tasks, the benefits of many-shot ICL only emerge after addressing the increased noise and uncertainty from longer inputs.
Many-shot ICL enables LLMs to concentrate more logit mass on the correct answer and amplify the disparity between correct and incorrect options.
The quality of uncertainty measures (as indicated by AUROC) remains high across different shot counts.
papers.limitation:
Exclusion of open-ended tasks such as summarization and translation due to lack of robust uncertainty quantification techniques.
Limited exploration of other ICL paradigms like unsupervised ICL, reinforced ICL, and chain-of-thought prompting.
future_direction: Applying uncertainty quantification methodologies to open-ended generative tasks.
Extending uncertainty analysis to reasoning-intensive contexts like chain-of-thought prompting.
Broadening the applicability of ICL in high-stakes domains.
papers.abstract: Recent advances in handling long sequences have facilitated the exploration of long-context in-context learning (ICL). While much of the existing research emphasizes performance improvements driven by additional in-context examples, the influence on the trustworthiness of generated responses remains underexplored. This paper addresses this gap by investigating how increased examples influence predictive uncertainty, an essential aspect in trustworthiness. We begin by systematically quantifying the uncertainty of ICL with varying shot counts, analyzing the impact of example quantity. Through uncertainty decomposition, we introduce a novel perspective on performance enhancement, with a focus on epistemic uncertainty (EU). Our results reveal that additional examples reduce total uncertainty in both simple and complex tasks by injecting task-specific knowledge, thereby diminishing EU and enhancing performance. For complex tasks, these advantages emerge only after addressing the increased noise and uncertainty associated with longer inputs. Finally, we explore the evolution of internal confidence across layers, unveiling the mechanisms driving the reduction in uncertainty.

papers.title: Attention Reallocation: Towards Zero-cost and Controllable Hallucination Mitigation of MLLMs
papers.research_question: Is it possible to mitigate MLLM hallucinations and improve the performance with nearly zero extra cost, without utilizing additional data or increasing decoding steps?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes attention reallocation (AttnReal), a training-free method to mitigate hallucinations in MLLMs by reallocating attention from output tokens to visual tokens, achieving nearly zero extra inference cost and a controllable trade-off between faithfulness and overall performance.
papers.conclusion: AttnReal is an effective, efficient, and controllable method for hallucination mitigation in MLLMs, requiring no extra data or training and minimal inference cost.
papers.key_findings:
Unreasonable attention allocation in MLLMs, where attention to historical output tokens increases while attention to visual tokens decreases, leads to output-dominated features and hallucinations.
AttnReal mitigates hallucinations by recycling excessive attention from output token 'sinks' and reallocating it uniformly to visual tokens.
AttnReal achieves a wide-range, controllable trade-off between response faithfulness (lower CHAIR scores) and overall performance (higher F1 scores).
AttnReal is plug-and-play, effective across six open-source MLLMs and three decoding strategies (Greedy, Beam Search, Nucleus Sampling).
AttnReal introduces minimal additional inference overhead compared to contrastive decoding or multi-candidate methods.
papers.abstract: Multi-Modal Large Language Models (MLLMs) stand out in various tasks but still struggle with hallucinations. While recent training-free mitigation methods mostly introduce additional inference overhead via retrospection strategy and contrastive decoding, we propose attention reallocation (AttnReal) to mitigate hallucinations with nearly zero extra cost. Our approach is motivated by the key observations that, MLLM's unreasonable attention distribution causes features to be dominated by historical output tokens, which further contributes to hallucinated responses because of the distribution gap between different token types. Based on the observations, AttnReal recycles excessive attention from output tokens and reallocates it to visual tokens, which reduces MLLM's reliance on language priors and ensures the decoding process depends more on the visual inputs. More interestingly, we find that, by controlling the intensity of AttnReal, we can achieve a wide-range trade-off between the response faithfulness and overall performance. Comprehensive results from different benchmarks validate the effectiveness of AttnReal across six open-source MLLMs and three decoding strategies.

papers.title: Response Uncertainty and Probe Modeling: Two Sides of the Same Coin in LLM Interpretability?
papers.research_question: What is the relationship between LLM response uncertainty and probe performance? Specifically, does a correlation exist, and what mechanisms underlie it?
papers.core_contribution: This paper demonstrates a strong negative correlation between LLM response uncertainty and probe performance, and provides a feature-attribution-based explanation showing that higher uncertainty corresponds to more dispersed important features, making probing harder.
papers.conclusion: The paper demonstrates a strong correlation between LLM response uncertainty and probe performance, with higher uncertainty linked to more dispersed important features, making probing harder. It also shows examples where low uncertainty corresponds to interpretable embeddings.
papers.key_findings:
There is a strong negative correlation between response uncertainty and probe performance across multiple datasets and LLMs.
High response uncertainty is associated with a larger set of important features in the LLM's representations, which hinders probe performance.
The probe model and LLM generation rely on similar sets of features, as shown by feature removal experiments.
The correlation is robust to variations in generation temperature, sliding window parameters, and prompt templates.
Using response uncertainty, examples where LLM embeddings align with human knowledge (e.g., brand categories, time cycles) can be identified.
papers.limitation:
The relationship between probe weights and prompt embeddings is not well understood.
The correlation is only observed in instruction-tuned models, not base LLMs.
The encoding and decoding processes for concepts are not fully understood.
A unified interpretability framework is needed.
future_direction: Investigating the analogy between prompts and probes.
Studying parameter changes during instruction tuning.
Developing a unified interpretability framework.
papers.abstract: Probing techniques have shown promise in revealing how LLMs encode human-interpretable concepts, particularly when applied to curated datasets. However, the factors governing a dataset's suitability for effective probe training are not well-understood. This study hypothesizes that probe performance on such datasets reflects characteristics of both the LLM's generated responses and its internal feature space. Through quantitative analysis of probe performance and LLM response uncertainty across a series of tasks, we find a strong correlation: improved probe performance consistently corresponds to a reduction in response uncertainty, and vice versa. Subsequently, we delve deeper into this correlation through the lens of feature importance analysis. Our findings indicate that high LLM response variance is associated with a larger set of important features, which poses a greater challenge for probe models and often results in diminished performance. Moreover, leveraging the insights from response uncertainty analysis, we are able to identify concrete examples where LLM representations align with human knowledge across diverse domains, offering additional evidence of interpretable reasoning in LLMs.

papers.title: Mirage in the Eyes: Hallucination Attack on Multi-modal Large Language Models with Only Attention Sink
papers.research_question: This paper investigates how attention sink phenomena in Multi-modal Large Language Models (MLLMs) are linked to hallucination and proposes a method to exploit this for adversarial attacks.
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces a hallucination attack that exploits attention sink behaviors in MLLMs to trigger hallucinated content, demonstrating vulnerabilities in current models and their mitigation strategies.
papers.conclusion: The study reveals that attention sink behaviors in MLLMs can be exploited to induce hallucinations, highlighting critical vulnerabilities and the need for improved defenses.
papers.key_findings:
Attention sink tokens aggregate misleading global information and are linked to hallucinated responses in MLLMs.
The proposed hallucination attack effectively increases hallucination rates in various MLLMs.
The attack is transferable to black-box models and commercial APIs like GPT-4o and Gemini 1.5.
It successfully bypasses existing mitigation strategies such as OPERA, VCD, and others.
The attack maintains the quality of model responses, making it stealthy and practical.
papers.abstract: Fusing visual understanding into language generation, Multi-modal Large Language Models (MLLMs) are revolutionizing visual-language applications. Yet, these models are often plagued by the hallucination problem, which involves generating inaccurate objects, attributes, and relationships that do not match the visual content. In this work, we delve into the internal attention mechanisms of MLLMs to reveal the underlying causes of hallucination, exposing the inherent vulnerabilities in the instruction-tuning process. We propose a novel hallucination attack against MLLMs that exploits attention sink behaviors to trigger hallucinated content with minimal image-text relevance, posing a significant threat to critical downstream applications. Distinguished from previous adversarial methods that rely on fixed patterns, our approach generates dynamic, effective, and highly transferable visual adversarial inputs, without sacrificing the quality of model responses. Comprehensive experiments on 6 prominent MLLMs demonstrate the efficacy of our attack in compromising black-box MLLMs even with extensive mitigating mechanisms, as well as the promising results against cutting-edge commercial APIs, such as GPT-4o and Gemini 1.5. Our code is available at https://huggingface.co/RachelHGF/Mirage-in-the-Eyes.

papers.title: Strong hallucinations from negation and how to fix them
papers.research_question: How do language models handle negation and why do they produce strong hallucinations? How can we fix these hallucinations?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces a hybrid method (Λ) that treats negation as an operation over latent representations, constraining the evolution of distributions to eliminate strong hallucinations and improve performance on tasks with negation without requiring negative data.
papers.conclusion: The hybrid approach Λ effectively reduces strong hallucinations from negation and improves model performance on logical tasks by constraining the LM's distribution to respect logical semantics.
papers.key_findings:
Language models inevitably produce strong hallucinations due to their distribution over strings not respecting logical properties, as proven theoretically.
The proposed method Λ improves performance on masked knowledge retrieval (MKR) and natural language inference (NLI) tasks with negation.
Λ achieves 0 exact matches on MKR and significant accuracy improvements on NLI (e.g., 13% on one NLI dataset, 91% on another).
Λ uses models fine-tuned only on positive data, avoiding the need for sparse negative data.
Fine-tuned Llama combined with Λ showed a 27% accuracy improvement over Llama alone on ¬SNLI.
papers.limitation:
Tasks with long string output are beyond the paper's scope due to complex evaluations required.
Prompting procedures for Llama were unstable, with slight variations producing quite different results.
papers.abstract: Despite great performance on many tasks, language models (LMs) still struggle with reasoning, sometimes providing responses that cannot possibly be true because they stem from logical incoherence. We call such responses \textit{strong hallucinations} and prove that they follow from an LM's computation of its internal representations for logical operators and outputs from those representations. Focusing on negation, we provide a novel solution in which negation is treated not as another element of a latent representation, but as \textit{an operation over an LM's latent representations that constrains how they may evolve}. We show that our approach improves model performance in cloze prompting and natural language inference tasks with negation without requiring training on sparse negative data.

papers.title: Look Closer! An Adversarial Parametric Editing Framework for Hallucination Mitigation in VLMs
papers.research_question: How can we mitigate hallucinations in Vision-Language Models (VLMs) by editing critical parameters in an adversarial parametric editing framework?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes ALEAHallu, an adversarial parametric editing framework for hallucination mitigation in VLMs, which follows an activate-locate-edit adversarially paradigm and edits only critical parameter clusters.
papers.conclusion: ALEAHallu effectively mitigates hallucinations in VLMs by editing a minimal parameter subset, enhancing visual attention, and imposing no additional inference overhead.
papers.key_findings:
ALEAHallu reduces object hallucinations (lower CHAIR scores) while maintaining or improving recall on image caption and VQA tasks.
The method increases the model's attention to visual tokens, as shown by attention visualization.
Ablation studies show that editing and constraint losses, correct layer localization, and prefix tuning are all important components.
The edited model generalizes well across different datasets (MSCOCO, A-OKVQA, GQA).
The method does not add inference overhead and is efficient.
papers.limitation: Over-mitigation of hallucinations could limit expressive potential in creative domains.
future_direction: Integrate curriculum learning to further explore the performance ceiling of knowledge editing for hallucination suppression in VLMs.
papers.abstract: While Vision-Language Models (VLMs) have garnered increasing attention in the AI community due to their promising practical applications, they exhibit persistent hallucination issues, generating outputs misaligned with visual inputs. Recent studies attribute these hallucinations to VLMs' over-reliance on linguistic priors and insufficient visual feature integration, proposing heuristic decoding calibration strategies to mitigate them. However, the non-trainable nature of these strategies inherently limits their optimization potential. To this end, we propose an adversarial parametric editing framework for Hallucination mitigation in VLMs, which follows an \textbf{A}ctivate-\textbf{L}ocate-\textbf{E}dit \textbf{A}dversarially paradigm. Specifically, we first construct an activation dataset that comprises grounded responses (positive samples attentively anchored in visual features) and hallucinatory responses (negative samples reflecting LLM prior bias and internal knowledge artifacts). Next, we identify critical hallucination-prone parameter clusters by analyzing differential hidden states of response pairs. Then, these clusters are fine-tuned using prompts injected with adversarial tuned prefixes that are optimized to maximize visual neglect, thereby forcing the model to prioritize visual evidence over inherent parametric biases. Evaluations on both generative and discriminative VLM tasks demonstrate the significant effectiveness of ALEAHallu in alleviating hallucinations. Our code is available at https://github.com/hujiayu1223/ALEAHallu.

papers.title: Overthinking the Truth: Understanding how Language Models Process False Demonstrations
papers.research_question: Why do language models imitate incorrect demonstrations in their context, and how does this behavior emerge internally?
papers.core_contribution: Language models 'overthink' when given false few-shot demonstrations, and this harmful imitation is caused by specific 'false induction heads' in late layers that attend to and copy incorrect labels from the context.
papers.conclusion: Studying intermediate model computations, such as through the logit lens and head ablation, is a promising avenue for understanding and mitigating harmful context-following behaviors.
papers.key_findings:
Given incorrect demonstrations, model accuracy decreases in later layers after a 'critical layer', a phenomenon termed 'overthinking'.
Ablating late layers or specific attention heads improves accuracy on incorrect demonstrations, indicating these components are responsible for the harmful imitation.
False induction heads are identified as attention heads in late layers that attend to and promote false labels from previous demonstrations.
Ablating a small set of false induction heads reduces the accuracy gap between correct and incorrect prompts by an average of 38.9% across 14 datasets.
The overthinking phenomenon and the role of false induction heads are consistent across multiple model families and sizes.
future_direction: Building tools to understand intermediate computations to proactively understand and reduce harmful model behaviors.
Applying insights to detect and guard against prompt injection attacks.
papers.abstract: Modern language models can imitate complex patterns through few-shot learning, enabling them to complete challenging tasks without fine-tuning. However, imitation can also lead models to reproduce inaccuracies or harmful content if present in the context. We study harmful imitation through the lens of a model's internal representations, and identify two related phenomena: "overthinking" and "false induction heads". The first phenomenon, overthinking, appears when we decode predictions from intermediate layers, given correct vs. incorrect few-shot demonstrations. At early layers, both demonstrations induce similar model behavior, but the behavior diverges sharply at some "critical layer", after which the accuracy given incorrect demonstrations progressively decreases. The second phenomenon, false induction heads, are a possible mechanistic cause of overthinking: these are heads in late layers that attend to and copy false information from previous demonstrations, and whose ablation reduces overthinking. Beyond scientific understanding, our results suggest that studying intermediate model computations could be a promising avenue for understanding and guarding against harmful model behaviors.

papers.title: PoLLMgraph: Unraveling Hallucinations in Large Language Models via State Transition Dynamics
papers.research_question: The paper investigates whether hallucinations in large language models can be effectively detected by analyzing the model's internal state transition dynamics using probabilistic models.
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces PoLLMgraph, a white-box method that detects hallucinations in LLMs by modeling internal state transition dynamics using probabilistic models, achieving state-of-the-art performance with significant improvements over existing methods.
papers.conclusion: PoLLMgraph is an effective white-box method for detecting hallucinations in LLMs by leveraging state transition dynamics within activation patterns, and its empirical success demonstrates potential for safeguarding LLMs from generating hallucinated content.
papers.key_findings:
PoLLMgraph outperforms existing black-box, gray-box, and white-box methods by a considerable margin, evidenced by over 20% improvement in AUC-ROC on benchmark datasets like TruthfulQA.
The method is highly data-efficient, requiring fewer than 100 annotated training samples to achieve strong performance.
PoLLMgraph generalizes across different LLM architectures (decoder-only and encoder-decoder) and is robust to distribution shifts to some extent.
The Hidden Markov Model (HMM) variant of PoLLMgraph consistently outperforms the Markov Model (MM) variant, indicating the benefit of latent state modeling.
The method's performance is sensitive to hyperparameters like the number of abstract states and PCA dimensions, but it plateaus at reasonable settings.
papers.limitation:
The hyperparameter settings are crucial for identifying hallucination behavior based on state transition dynamics, and the state abstraction is closely related to modeling the hallucination patterns from internal activations.
The generalizability of PoLLMgraph needs further validation with larger distribution shifts, varied LLM architectures, and broader datasets, especially when the reference and testing data have very different semantics or when the LLM undergoes fine-tuning causing concept shifts.
future_direction: Exploring scenarios with a larger degree of distribution shifts between reference and testing data.
Conducting more comprehensive experiments with varied LLM architectures and broader datasets to enhance validation of generalizability.
papers.abstract: Despite tremendous advancements in large language models (LLMs) over recent years, a notably urgent challenge for their practical deployment is the phenomenon of hallucination, where the model fabricates facts and produces non-factual statements. In response, we propose PoLLMgraph, a Polygraph for LLMs, as an effective model-based white-box detection and forecasting approach. PoLLMgraph distinctly differs from the large body of existing research that concentrates on addressing such challenges through black-box evaluations. In particular, we demonstrate that hallucination can be effectively detected by analyzing the LLM's internal state transition dynamics during generation via tractable probabilistic models. Experimental results on various open-source LLMs confirm the efficacy of PoLLMgraph, outperforming state-of-the-art methods by a considerable margin, evidenced by over 20% improvement in AUC-ROC on common benchmarking datasets like TruthfulQA. Our work paves a new way for model-based white-box analysis of LLMs, motivating the research community to further explore, understand, and refine the intricate dynamics of LLM behaviors.

papers.title: The Hidden Uncertainty in a Neural Networks Activations
papers.research_question: Does the distribution of a neural network's latent representations correlate with epistemic and aleatoric uncertainty, and can it be used to estimate uncertainty without modifying the training procedure?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces a framework for estimating both epistemic and aleatoric uncertainty from the latent representations of neural networks without modifying the training procedure, showing that deeper layers yield uncertainty estimates similar to established methods like MC Dropout and Deep Ensembles.
papers.conclusion: The hidden activations of neural networks contain information about both aleatoric and epistemic uncertainty. Uncertainty proxies derived from density estimates of deep layers closely follow those of established methods, enabling wide application and rapid deployment without retraining.
papers.key_findings:
Epistemic uncertainty can be identified with the negative log-likelihood (surprise) of observing a particular latent representation.
Aleatoric uncertainty can be quantified via the entropy of the predictive distribution derived from output-conditional latent densities.
Deeper layers yield epistemic uncertainty estimates that behave similarly to established but computationally expensive methods (e.g., MC Dropout, Deep Ensembles).
Shallow layers yield more conservative epistemic uncertainty estimates, which are better for out-of-distribution detection but worse for calibration near the training data distribution.
Additional regularization (e.g., a reconstruction loss) improves out-of-distribution detection performance but leads to ambiguous calibration close to the training data distribution.
papers.limitation:
Feature collapse can make activations of out-of-distribution data indistinguishable from training data.
High-dimensional densities are challenging to estimate.
Additional regularization improves out-of-distribution detection but leads to ambiguous calibration near the training data distribution.
future_direction: Aggregating uncertainty information from several layers for out-of-distribution detection.
papers.abstract: The distribution of a neural network's latent representations has been successfully used to detect out-of-distribution (OOD) data. This work investigates whether this distribution moreover correlates with a model's epistemic uncertainty, thus indicates its ability to generalise to novel inputs. We first empirically verify that epistemic uncertainty can be identified with the surprise, thus the negative log-likelihood, of observing a particular latent representation. Moreover, we demonstrate that the output-conditional distribution of hidden representations also allows quantifying aleatoric uncertainty via the entropy of the predictive distribution. We analyse epistemic and aleatoric uncertainty inferred from the representations of different layers and conclude that deeper layers lead to uncertainty with similar behaviour as established - but computationally more expensive - methods (e.g. deep ensembles). While our approach does not require modifying the training process, we follow prior work and experiment with an additional regularising loss that increases the information in the latent representations. We find that this leads to improved OOD detection of epistemic uncertainty at the cost of ambiguous calibration close to the data distribution. We verify our findings on both classification and regression models.

papers.title: Context-Aware Decoding for Faithful Vision-Language Generation
papers.research_question: How do layer-wise generation dynamics drive hallucinations in large vision-language models, and how can we mitigate them with a training-free strategy?
papers.core_contribution: The paper discovers a commitment-depth gap between truthful and hallucinatory tokens in LVLMs and introduces Context Embedding Injection, a training-free method that uses the context embedding as a grounding signal to reduce hallucinations.
papers.conclusion: The layer-wise study revealed that truthful tokens commit earlier across decoder layers than hallucinatory ones, highlighting commitment depth as an interpretable signal of visual faithfulness. Leveraging this finding, the proposed Context Embedding Injection (CEI) achieves consistent reductions in hallucination while maintaining comparable coverage, demonstrating its effectiveness and generality.
papers.key_findings:
Truthful tokens exhibit higher semantic alignment with the context embedding than hallucinatory tokens.
Truthful tokens accumulate probability mass on their final candidates earlier across decoder layers than hallucinatory ones, revealing a commitment-depth gap.
Context Embedding Injection (CEI) reduces hallucination rates on CHAIR, AMBER, and MMHal-Bench benchmarks.
Dynamic CEI, which adapts injection strength based on mean top-K probability mass, yields the lowest overall hallucination rates.
CEI maintains visual fidelity in open-ended generation without sacrificing coverage or informativeness.
papers.limitation:
Dynamic CEI introduces computational overhead by requiring two forward passes per token, which may limit applicability in latency-sensitive settings.
Evaluation is limited to COCO-style benchmarks, leaving open questions about generalization to specialized domains (e.g., medical imaging, autonomous driving).
Mechanistic analyses depend on externally provided token-level hallucination labels, which may limit the range of settings for similar analyses.
CEI requires white-box access to internal representations and the unembedding matrix, limiting direct applicability to closed-source LVLMs.
future_direction: Extend the framework to multi-image or video grounding.
Explore integration with contrastive decoding.
Investigate commitment-aware steering for other multimodal reasoning tasks.
papers.abstract: Hallucinations, generating responses inconsistent with the visual input, remain a critical limitation of large vision-language models (LVLMs), especially in open-ended tasks such as image captioning and visual reasoning. In this work, we probe the layer-wise generation dynamics that drive hallucinations and propose a training-free mitigation strategy. Employing the Logit Lens, we examine how LVLMs construct next-token distributions across decoder layers, uncovering a pronounced commitment-depth gap: truthful tokens accumulate probability mass on their final candidates earlier than hallucinatory ones. Drawing on this discovery, we introduce Context Embedding Injection (CEI), a lightweight method that harnesses the hidden state of the last input token-the context embedding-as a grounding signal to maintain visual fidelity throughout decoding and curb hallucinations. Evaluated on the CHAIR, AMBER, and MMHal-Bench benchmarks (with a maximum token length of 512), CEI outperforms state-of-the-art baselines across three LVLMs, with its dynamic variant yielding the lowest overall hallucination rates. By integrating novel mechanistic insights with a scalable intervention, this work advances the mitigation of hallucinations in LVLMs.

papers.title: Tethered Reasoning: Decoupling Entropy from Hallucination in Quantized LLMs via Manifold Steering
papers.research_question: How can high-temperature inference in quantized language models be enabled without hallucination by decoupling output entropy from trajectory divergence through geometric tethering?
papers.core_contribution: Helix is a geometric framework that uses a Unified Truth Score and manifold steering to enable temperature-invariant reasoning in quantized LLMs, reducing hallucination while maintaining accuracy and unlocking creative diversity at high temperatures.
papers.conclusion: Helix addresses trajectory divergence through geometric tethering, enabling reliable high-temperature inference in quantized models and revealing a High-Entropy Creative Reservoir for increased creative diversity.
papers.key_findings:
Helix enables 4-bit quantized Granite 4.0 H Small to exceed the full-precision baseline on GSM8K, achieving 91.80% accuracy at T=1.0 compared to 87.27%.
Temperature-invariant reasoning is achieved with minimal degradation: GSM8K accuracy degrades only 2.81pp from T=0.5 to T=3.0, and MMLU only 1.24pp degradation.
High-Entropy Creative Reservoir is revealed, with duplication dropping to 5-20% at high temperatures versus 70-80% at low temperatures, enabling multi-temperature synthesis for 200%+ more unique concepts.
Steering sparse Transformer attention layers is sufficient to correct drift in hybrid SSM-Transformer architectures, suggesting a new paradigm for control.
UTS provides real-time per-token uncertainty telemetry, with steering affecting only 0.2-2.5% of tokens.
papers.limitation:
Primary evaluation on Granite 4.0, with cross-validation only on Qwen3.
Benchmark coverage limited to GSM8K, HumanEval, MMLU, and creative ideation.
Manifold constructed from generic prompts.
Creativity evaluation relies on semantic similarity and LLM-based judging.
The High-Entropy Creative Reservoir is an emergent phenomenon observed in temperature sweep experiments without systematic study.
future_direction: Cross-Architecture Steering Dynamics: Adapting manifold construction to explicitly model Expert Routing Uncertainty in MoE architectures.
Semantic Pattern Classifiers: Developing lightweight failure-mode classifiers for interventions.
Uncertainty Admission Protocols: Implementing a rejection option for extreme manifold distance.
papers.abstract: Quantized language models face a fundamental dilemma: low sampling temperatures yield repetitive, mode-collapsed outputs, while high temperatures (T > 2.0) cause trajectory divergence and semantic incoherence. We present HELIX, a geometric framework that decouples output entropy from hallucination by tethering hidden-state trajectories to a pre-computed truthfulness manifold. HELIX computes a Unified Truth Score (UTS) combining token-level semantic entropy with Mahalanobis distance from the manifold. When UTS indicates trajectory divergence, graduated steering vectors redirect activations toward structurally coherent regions while affecting only 0.2-2.5% of tokens. On 4-bit quantized Granite 4.0 H Small (32B/9B active, hybrid Mamba-Transformer): GSM8K maintains 88.84% accuracy at T = 3.0 (2.81pp degradation from T = 0.5); MMLU maintains 72.49% across 14,042 questions (1.24pp degradation). This demonstrates that high-temperature hallucination is primarily trajectory divergence rather than semantic collapse. Notably, steering the sparse Transformer attention layers (~10% of layers) is sufficient to correct drift in the Mamba-2 state-space formulation. Geometric tethering reveals a previously-masked High-Entropy Creative Reservoir. At T > 2.0, steered outputs exhibit 5-20% idea duplication versus 70-80% at conservative settings. Cross-architecture validation (Qwen3-30B-A3B MOE) confirms this phenomenon is architecture-independent, with 46.7% higher unique concept generation. HELIX acts as a syntax tether, enabling exploration of semantic diversity without violating the logical backbone required for valid output. This enables Multi-Temperature Synthesis, generating 200% more unique concepts than single-temperature inference.

papers.title: Revis: Sparse Latent Steering to Mitigate Object Hallucination in Large Vision-Language Models
papers.research_question: How can object hallucination in Large Vision-Language Models be mitigated by reactivating suppressed visual information through sparse latent steering?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces REVIS, a training-free framework that uses orthogonal projection to decouple visual information from language priors in the latent space and performs sparse intervention at an optimal layer to mitigate object hallucination in LVLMs.
papers.conclusion: REVIS effectively mitigates object hallucination in LVLMs by reactivating visual information via sparse latent steering, without compromising general reasoning capabilities or inference efficiency.
papers.key_findings:
REVIS reduces object hallucination rates by approximately 19% compared to state-of-the-art baselines while preserving general reasoning capabilities.
Orthogonal projection is necessary to decouple visual information from entangled language priors, preventing model collapse that occurs with naive steering vectors.
Sparse intervention at a single, optimally selected layer is sufficient and more efficient than dense multi-layer intervention.
The method maintains inference efficiency, adding negligible latency compared to contrastive decoding methods that require multiple forward passes.
REVIS generalizes effectively across diverse LVLM architectures (Qwen, LLaVA, InternVL series).
papers.limitation:
REVIS relies on the base model's representations, limiting its ability to rectify absolute perceptual blindness.
The evaluation focuses on object hallucination and does not cover other types of hallucinations (e.g., attribute, relation).
future_direction: Extending the method to other types of hallucinations (attribute, relation).
Exploring its application in more complex multimodal tasks.
papers.abstract: Despite the advanced capabilities of Large Vision-Language Models (LVLMs), they frequently suffer from object hallucination. One reason is that visual features and pretrained textual representations often become intertwined in the deeper network layers. To address this, we propose REVIS, a training-free framework designed to explicitly re-activate this suppressed visual information. Rooted in latent space geometry, REVIS extracts the pure visual information vector via orthogonal projection and employs a calibrated strategy to perform sparse intervention only at the precise depth where suppression occurs. This surgical approach effectively restores visual information with minimal computational cost. Empirical evaluations on standard benchmarks demonstrate that REVIS reduces object hallucination rates by approximately 19% compared to state-of-the-art baselines, while preserving general reasoning capabilities.

papers.title: Getting a CLUE: A Method for Explaining Uncertainty Estimates
papers.research_question: How can we interpret uncertainty estimates from probabilistic models by finding counterfactual explanations that indicate how to change an input to make the model more confident?
